Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Derek wrote:
>>Which isn't true. You can make equally vicious and cut-throat decks
under 4CL, and that will hurt the game's popularity with women just as
much. Attempting to blame NL is missing the ACTUAL problem.>>

This comes up a lot (not the 4CL, I'm staying far away from that...)--the idea
of "cut-throat" vs "fun" decks, and "playing for fun" vs "playing to win", and
I'm kind of interested in seeing other folks views on this.

When I play VTES, I play to win. Winning is not the be all and end all of the
game, and I am perfectly happy when I lose, and I certainly don't play like a
dick for the sake of winning (i.e. I suggest that people take back obviously
stupid moves, I don't hide my pool in a little cup, whatever), but I find that
I have a much better time with the game when I am playing to win, and my
opponents are playing to win. I like when my opponents are playing effective
decks that can sweep the table, and go out of their way to kill me (ya know,
without being dicks), and I like playing effective decks that can sweep the
table, and I try my darndest to kill my opponents. It isn't about *winning*, it
is all about *trying* to win.

When I play VTES, I'm not looking for role-playing (I'm not a role-player and I
have no interest in the Vampire RPG, except as source material for VTES), I'm
not looking for amusing new card combos (although I certainly appreciate good
ones), and I'm not looking to see lots of different cards (I've pretty much
seen them all already). I'm looking for a good, solid strategy game, where
there is interesting interaction between deck *strategies*, not cards (how does
Pot Rush work against Ventrue Bonding? How does Gangrel Wall of Untap work vs
Malk S+B?). I have no problem with my opponents using decks that have 20 of the
same card in them--I like to see how that affects their chances at winning, and
I make decks like that, 'cause they are effective (one of my best decks has 22
S:CE cards in it). When my opponent plays Conditioning for the 13th time, my
reaction is not "Man. Play a different card.", it is "Man. How do I make my
deck more effective so it can deal with an opponent using13 Conditionings."

When I play with people who have different victory conditions that I do (i.e.
I'm trying get victory points, they are trying to get 12 Werewolf Packs into
play), neither of us have a good time--they feel screwed 'cause they didn't get
off their goofy card combo, and I feel screwed 'cause my opponent wasn't really
trying. Thus, I prefer to play with folks who have the same view of the game as
I do.

Where do the rest of y'all stand here?

Peter D Bakija

First problem. Quite a lot of gamers are willing to do this. I've
seen it more in other games, but it'll creep into V:TES more and more
as we get a larger following.

And worse, about the only thing you can do for it is to smack each

>stupid moves, I don't hide my pool in a little cup, whatever), but I find that
>I have a much better time with the game when I am playing to win, and my
>opponents are playing to win. I like when my opponents are playing effective

The emphasis here needs to be "when EVERYONE is playing to win."

V:TES is a multiplayer game, and it has a multiplayer mechanic. The
prey-to-the-left theory helps quite a bit, but it still leaves one
problem; what happens when one person is not trying to win?

In a 4-player game, its problem is immediately seen; one person has
low pressure from their predator, and one person has low opposition
from their prey. The person who is NOT sitting next to the "dead
slot" is at an immediate, acute disadvantage. The chances of winning
lean heavily towards the person who is the predator of the "dead
slot", as he will basically get 1 VP with little opposition, and then
have the advantage of momentum.

This makes it difficult though, as the rabid opposition one will
receive for SUGGESTING that people should play to win demonstrates.
This isn't to say that everyone should play a tournament-quality deck
at all times, but maybe that each deck should perhaps have a CONCEPT
of "how to oust prey" and "how not to be ousted", at least. But some
people will even disagree with that, and say "i should be allowed to
make my 12-werewolf pack deck if i want to". OK, yep, you're allowed.
In an ideal world, there would be plenty of other players for you to
play with, and for me to play with, so that we don't have to frustrate
each other at the same table. But that ain't so yet... so we have
clashes of opinion. And those clashes of opinion are the second
problem.

>When I play VTES, I'm not looking for role-playing (I'm not a role-player and I
>have no interest in the Vampire RPG, except as source material for VTES), I'm

Third problem. The "pure strategy" approach actually appeals to very
few people; most everyone tends to want a something else out of the
game as well. What that may be is left to them.

>not looking for amusing new card combos (although I certainly appreciate good
>ones), and I'm not looking to see lots of different cards (I've pretty much
>seen them all already). I'm looking for a good, solid strategy game, where
>there is interesting interaction between deck *strategies*, not cards (how does
>Pot Rush work against Ventrue Bonding? How does Gangrel Wall of Untap work vs
>Malk S+B?). I have no problem with my opponents using decks that have 20 of the
>same card in them--I like to see how that affects their chances at winning, and
>I make decks like that, 'cause they are effective (one of my best decks has 22
>S:CE cards in it). When my opponent plays Conditioning for the 13th time, my
>reaction is not "Man. Play a different card.", it is "Man. How do I make my
>deck more effective so it can deal with an opponent using13 Conditionings."

I prefer to think of it in this fashion: Focus equals predictability.
If I think your deck has 13 Conditionings in it, I can assume that
every bleed is going to potentially be for 3 or more. This allows me
to construct my own strategy accordingly, and answers a lot of
questions that I would normally otherwise have ("is it worth the risk
this turn? maybe he doesn't have one. how much of a risk is it?"),
and so on.

Generally, duplicate cards beyond 10 or so carry their own inherent
flaws. Majesty is one such card - it's neat to have 16, and it means
that you can sure end combat and untap a whole lot, but what if you
never get into combat? Same with the bleed cards, etc. - if you have
13 Conditionings, but people keep blocking or bouncing your bleeds,
when will you ever get to play one to advantage?

About the only cards that do NOT carry inherent drawbacks are action
cards; they generally require only a vampire with the appropriate
discipline, and if you don't have one of those, you're already in
heaps of trouble. But the action cards themselves are rarely, if
ever, effective on their own... exceptions are things like Cryptic
Mission, Corruption, Jar the Soul, and Shadow Twin, which have a small
individual effect, built-in stealth, and produce a major effect over a
longer period of time. Such cards lend themselves well to the
30-in-a-deck idea.

It's difficult to get new players to understand this, though, when
they have a deck that's designed to get a bunch of Brujah on Sport
Bikes and beat hell out of everything, and they're sitting in front of
the Malk S&B deck that's carrying 10 Lost in Crowds, 10 Cloak the
Gatherings, and 10 Faceless Nights. In their view, the deck behind
them is stupid and broken, without realizing that their own deck just
HAPPENS to play into its hands perfectly.

Fourth problem; being able to explain that effectively.

>Where do the rest of y'all stand here?

On my feet?

-- Derek

I think I'm with you, except I'm a bit more about "winning with style."
I always TRY to win; the example of "get an Assault Rifle and Soul Gem on
Fransiscus" or somesuch as a "goal" cheezes me off, and don't even get me
started on "I'm just role-playing as a Malkavian!" players. My goal is to
get in there and get VPs, no matter what the deck.
But, after that, I've usually got some neat trick or combo that I'd like
to see, and work at it to make it VP-viable.
Usually, this gets me 0 to .5 VPs, but when I bring a deck "purely
designed to win," I make the finals.
For non-tournament play, I'm almost always trying some new "trick."
It's all about the deckbuilding and interaction, and doing it in a way that
no one else has. When I decide what deck to make and play, I'm ALL about
creativity, without losing the goal of viability. Once I'm in there and
playing, it's all about VPs, though. I like to get my "trick" off, but
usually because that's what makes the deck GO, and thereby start winning.
I'm not as in to pure table-sweepers, not that I don't try to sweep
tables every chance I get. I like winning, I guess, but I'd rather win in a
way that makes people say "Wow!" instead of "Fuck you!" =)

I put it this way: the game is designed with the understanding in mind that players
are trying to win. If players have some other motivation in mind, the rules don't
work right. It's like buying a car and then using it to pound nails: it might work
or it might not but it wasn't designed to pound nails. It was designed to drive.
Same with games designed for people to win. Just like a car, if you use it for what
it was designed for, you'll usually find that that's the way you get the most fun
out of it.

Fred

Messages.Author: Mark Allen
Messages.Body:
One thing that I find that kills the game is a player that just rolls over
and dies because they have to go somewhere or they foresee destruction or
whatever. If someone plays cheese, my goal basically comes down to how long
I stay in the game. There are different levels of victory but when people
give up because they realize they will not get a single VP, that is just
poor sportsmanship.

The other day I was playing in a 4 player game where my crosstable ally was
doing basically dick. Because of this, My predator was extra aggressive and
my prey was extremely defensive/stealthy. I was getting the shaft from both
sides. It was a bit upsetting and I mentioned something to my ally who
responded with 'I can't do anything because I don't have the cards'. At one
point my prey deflected a small bleed and my ally was ready to cream my vamp
for some reason just so he could 'play his killer combo'. After I ousted my
prey, he changed gears and let me run right over him, not even blocking my
actions.

The whole point here is that even though I ended up with the majority of the
victory points in the end, it was an empty victory. I really should have
only earned one VP. I won, but I didn't care because it was not my deck that
won or my great wisdom but because there was another player on the table
that did not have the dedication to play.

The point is that if my deck does even half of what its supposed to do like
call votes, bleed heavy or intercept, etc.. its a victory. No one I know
commends someone for playing a deck that sweeps but when someone plays an
original deck, eyebrows are raised

Let me tack this one on for my own personal opinion, too.

I tend to go after the stuff that people can't make win consistently,
and then to figure out why. Intercept has been a frequent appearance
in my tournament decks recently, because consistently making intercept
decks get more than "the last 2" VPs is a challenge. I like
challenges. Combat is an even bigger challenge, and my last run at a
bruise/bleed deck discovered that if enough vote decks are on the
table, you lose when they team up on you. Information noted.

But just because you see me sitting there with Omaya, Gunther,
Caitlin, and a couple Raven Spies doesn't mean that I'm intending to
go to my right all game. My qualifier deck's basic intent was "put
enough permanents, toys, Blood Dolls, etc. out that I can consistently
gain 4 pool per turn, and consistently intercept anything that happens
near me that I don't like." Its secondary intent was "now that I'm
gaining 4 pool per turn, get out my entire crypt and bleed for 1
lots." My goal is always to gain VPs. =)

>creativity, without losing the goal of viability. Once I'm in there and
>playing, it's all about VPs, though. I like to get my "trick" off, but
>usually because that's what makes the deck GO, and thereby start winning.
> I'm not as in to pure table-sweepers, not that I don't try to sweep
>tables every chance I get. I like winning, I guess, but I'd rather win in a
>way that makes people say "Wow!" instead of "Fuck you!" =)

Hm. About all I can say in support of that one is that I've played
the Crypt Machine twice in "real" competition in the 3 years since I
first played it. I knew after its first outing that it had a good
chance of sweeping any given table -- and I immediately retired it
from my own active play list, as I have several other decks that I
consider to be "sweep-quality".

While I have every confidence in bringing any of these decks to a
tournament, and would expect to reach the finals (after a small update
to include some Final Nights cards, of course), I will rarely do so.
Even if I'm playing the Continental Championships, it will STILL be a
tossup as to whether I play something "experimental-but-good", or
something "ridiculously good". I could, of course, play the
tried-and-true stuff like Minion Tap/5th with Big Obfuscate
Malkavians, who then wander around bleeding with Conditioning at +3
stealth. But such decks are very boring. Winning itself is nice, but
I prefer to have fun when I play... and ah, the thrill of winning with
something that ISN'T the tried-and-true formula. Or just the thrill
of realizing that your deck may not have won, but represented an
important advance in the search for HOW to win - and next time you'll
be able to use it.

Besides, there's always the knowledge that if you're going crosswise
to the typical "tournament metagame", you have a great chance of
catching a bunch of decks with their pants down. If any Minion
Tap/5th deck had been seated near me in Atlanta, they'd have been
toast; unfortunately, I think there were only 1 or 2 decks at the
whole qualifier who were using that combo, and I never saw any of them
even at my TABLE. d'oh! Bad luck for me.

-- Derek

Oh, don't get me wrong here--I'm certainly entertained by clever combos and

what goes with Meat Hook better than Garou?), but my decks are designed (in

irational stuff to protect my favorite vampires ("No! Not Ramona! Take me

Temptation of the Greater Power, or whatever, I say "That could have worked
better for me..." If someone kills me because they have a good deck, and I just

in. A shift in the metagame can suddenly make a really bad card playable as it
happens to mess over one or more of the new tier 1 decks.

I'm looking for a good, solid strategy game, where
>there is interesting interaction between deck *strategies*, not cards (how
>does
>Pot Rush work against Ventrue Bonding? How does Gangrel Wall of Untap work vs
>Malk S+B?).

This is probably where we differ the most. Match up analysis is interesting to
me on a theoretical level, but I'm far more interested in individual card
interactions when I'm playing games.

I have no problem with my opponents using decks that have 20 of
>the
>same card in them--I like to see how that affects their chances at winning,
>and
>I make decks like that, 'cause they are effective (one of my best decks has
>22
>S:CE cards in it). When my opponent plays Conditioning for the 13th time, my
>reaction is not "Man. Play a different card.", it is "Man. How do I make my
>deck more effective so it can deal with an opponent using13 Conditionings."

I don't mind seeing a lot of the same card if it is necessary to get a concept
to work - Corruption, for instance. But, I do find lots of copies of vanilla
cards like Conditioning or Majesty (course, S:CE is obnoxious because it
reduces deck diversity) to be boring. Also, as a related issue, I don't find
playing or playing against the same decks often to be interesting.

Pat mentions "winning with style". I'd go a step farther? Winning and losing
mean nothing to me by themselves. The reason I've gotten so heavily into CCGs
rather than other games is that the number of possible interactions is so much
higher than in other competitive games (games with winners). But, getting back
to the thrust of your post, if I don't try to play the game as well as
possible, which means trying to win, I'm invalidating those interactions. So,
if I have a good (serious, tournament, whatever the right word is) deck, I tend
to end up playing along your lines; the difference is that when I go to build
decks, they often won't be well built in terms of winning.

Messages.Author: legbiter
Messages.Body:
Well, the trite answer is that i ALWAYS play for fun. And since i like
winning better than losing, i ALWAYS play to win, too. But since there
are things more important than winning - eg one's sense of integrity,
friendship, showing new people the glory of our darkly-majestic game,
not having to sleep in the bath - i won't do ANYTHING to win. But it's
not solely how you play and your attitude that determines whether you
and others are going to have fun - it's everybody singing from the
same hymn-sheet. This is one of the reasons i like sealed deck so much
- everybody starts off with a similar pool of cards.

If i differ from Peter at all significantly, it's in admitting that i
like best of all to see a card or combo that i'd never have thought of
come up in a game; and perhaps also i'd make a distinction between
different forms of the game as it's played in different groups. For
example, it would be no fun at all for me to make killer decks for
playing with at home - Sarah and Michael don't actually have ANY
cards, so i make all the decks and they and guests get to choose what
they are going to play, while i pick one at random. This is to offset
the inevitable advantage that i know what the decks contain, while
they do not. Additionally, we tried playing really competitive decks
at home, and Sarah and Andrew didn't like it because at home we get
together to play Jyhad as a social occasion, and in this environment
it is really much more like a complicated board-game with role-playing
aspects bolted on and less like a strategy game.

i don't want to overstate the role-playing here, though. A CCG is, on
one level, an RPG with no GM where your deck is your character. But in
VTES you are NOT a malkavian [though you might PRETEND to be one] even
if all your minions are. You are an unimaginably ancient and
indestructible vampire completely above the petty nonsense of sects
and clans, motivated by inhuman notions of hatred, lust and power. All
this is in the basic game, but since it is a complicated card-based
strategy game too there are opportunities to subvert the structure and
to play on a much higher and more abstract level. i like this too, and
play this way in non-home playgroups and tournaments, but i'm quite
clear that these are, and should be, different fora. Thus it is that i
can have quality fun at home, in the local playgroups and at
tournaments, and not sleep in the bath.

Messages.Author: Tim Eijpe
Messages.Body:
[snip exellent post]

Peter, I could not agree more.

I also think that it doesn't matter what kind of deck you play, which
cards are in it, or whether you play focussed, toolbox, NL or CL. It
is all about *intention* No matter what you play, you should attempt
to maximize your VP's or die trying. When I play I try to win, or
better to maximize my VP amount. That is MY way of fun. (I am just a
competative bastard)
Now I have been called too focussed on winning, degenerative and that
I take away the other players' fun. I can understand that from their
point of view, most of our playgroup play for fun and as a way to
relax. Which is a way of playing the game. NOT my way.
IU know I cannot change their way of playing an d sometimes adapt to
their playstyle, e.c.g. play a nonfocussed, "fun"deck (like the
!brujah Waste Vote deck). Still no matter what the deck, which players
sit at the table, my intention is to achieve as many vp's as possible
in the current game (which can be none, or a sweep).
I am not saying that every game should be cuthroat, final-like games.
But I feel that all players at least should have the decency to try
and win. That way there are no problems between the players. I mean a
situation with a play-to-win player and a have-fun player is a no win
situation for them both. I do feel that it is important that people
play *any* game according to the rules, which clearly state that the
object of the game is to gather as many vp's as possible in any given
game. This should be represented in deck design, playstyle and
intentions. I know I rather die trying in a good competative game,
than have a simple sweep due to the lack of intention. My most
enjoyable games are games in which we all play to win, and I end up
with 0 vp's due to the fact that someone else simply kicks my ass.
That way you become better players, think about the game and stop
making stupid mistakes.

Just my thoughts,

Tim Eijpe

Messages.Author: Matt Latham
Messages.Body:
First, lets clear up some perception issues. Both Peter's Camp (which
includes the chairman of VEKN, which pretty much means people like me
have no place in the NWO of VEKN tourney Jyhad. Makes me sad) and mine
are using unfair stereotyping characterizations. I'll outline them
below.

Peter depicts anyone with a deck concept that doesn't fit his mold of
play as a little kid who will stomp his feet and get mad when his 7
card combat combo or 12 Werewolf packs don't come out.

I depict players with decks like Peter advocates as imaginationless
cheeze-weasels who must win at any cost to validate themselves rather
than just play a damn GAME.

Both are extremes. A player or two at a given tourney will fit Peter's
definition and a player or two may fit mine, and the bulk of the
players fall in the middle.

So, if we can both acknowledge that few people fit my depiction AND
few people fit his depiction then we're better off as a community.

Ok, that said, what I wish for every tourney is that the people at
Peters end of the spectrum could move a smidge to the Derek philosophy
and thereby make the game 1000000 times better.

The Derek side (also props to Pat):

Quoth Derek:

Winning itself is nice, butI prefer to have fun when I play... and ah,

the thrill of winning with something that ISN'T the tried-and-true
formula. Or just the thrill of realizing that your deck may not have
won, but represented an
important advance in the search for HOW to win - and next time you'll
be able to use it.

End Quoth:

CCG's have two parts to their game: Deck construction and Play Skill.
Magic, as a game, no longer rewards the first aspect. Players get
their decks off the Net as generated by a handful of players and use
them at tourneys. The winner at the end of the day is the one who had
the best matchups and for the most part showed the best Play skill

Prior to last year, the Jyhad community rewarded both aspects via peer
approval. I won quite a few big tourneys "in my day" and what made the
wins special is the 18-20 people who shook my hand after each table
and said "Thats a really neat deck. Good luck at the next table. Can I
see the whole deck when you are done?"

I gain no joy from seeing a player with 22 S:CE cards. I gain no joy
from seeing a person with 22 stealth cards and 22 bleed modifiers. I
gain no joy because these people have decided to throw away a whole
aspect of the game (the deck construction portion) by using a cookie
cutter deck.

And yes Robert, I believe that these decks are infinitely easier to
build than the more creative decks that I have used and have had used
against me.

I am going to continue to laud the people like Derek who choose to win
with creativity and style, and I am going to continue to feel decks
like the ones Peter advocates kills a bit of the spirit of the game,
because every new player than emulates the cookie-cutter winner is
another person who will ignore the first aspect of Jyhad.

Don't give up on style. Please please please.

Matt

But where do you draw the line? How is it ok to have 15 Corruptions ("I need it

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Ian wrote:
>>It comes up because some cards are superior to others. I remember a very
long
thread for another game where everyone tried to define what cheesy meant. It's
a bit of "I know it when I see it", but the way I try to describe it is any
strategy that consistently does well without putting much thought into devising
it and/or does well when played by a bad player.>>

See, and that is where I see a problem--that people try to define "cheesy" at
all. Everyone has (theoretically) the same access to the basic components of
the game. Yes, some cards *are* superior to others--why is it my (or anyone's)
responsibility to *not* use these cards and not build the most effective
possible decks? If there are cards that are too good, it is the responsibility
of the players to make this known to the game designers, and it is the
responsibility of the game designers to fix things, bit I don't really see it
as a players responsibility to not use the powerful cards simply because somone
might think it was "cheesy".

How do you define a strategy that consistiently does well without putting much
thought into devising it and/or does well when played by a bad player? What is
such a strategy? One might think Malkavian S+B right off the bat, but I would
challenge someone to make a really good Malk S+B deck that can consistiently
win, in the hands of a bad player, in a well developed play environment (i.e.
an environment where the deck is just as likely to run into, for example, a
strong intercept deck, a bounce deck, a speedy bleed deck, a rush deck, or a
rampant pool gain deck).

The main problem with the concept of "cheesy" (among the many others) is that
it is completely subjective ("I can't describe it but I know it when I see
it"), and I, for one, am not interested in trying to avoid building decks that
might be deemed "cheesy" by a random subjective observer. I build decks that
are effective and legal, and I hope that my opponents are doing the same thing.
Yeah, sometimes my decks are funny, sometimes they aren't, but I always try to
make them effective without regard to what is or is not "cheesy".



easy win.

Messages.Author: Ben Peal
Messages.Body:
In Boston, we like to play both for "fun" and to "win". However,
we've found that it's no fun for anyone if we get a table of mixed
"fun" decks and tournament-caliber decks. So, we'll ask before we
play how strong the decks we're playing are, and then match up
accordingly. For the most part, we just play "fun" decks at our
gaming nights, but every so often people want to test out tournament
decks.

As much as I enjoy tournament play and "playing to win", I've found
that with tournament decks, you're only ever really using 10-20% of
your card collection. The rest of your collection - being deemed not
tournament worthy - ends up sitting on a shelf and collecting dust.
Why let the other 80-90% go to waste? Build some "fun" decks, play
some no-stress, non-competitive games, and put those cards to use.
Every so often you'll dig up a card that has tournament potential,
too.

I think there's also something to be said for not bringing your "A"
game against less-experienced players. There isn't much for them to
learn from getting the crap kicked out of them, and you might end up
discouraging them from playing. However, if you bring a less potent
deck and ease back on your opponents, you can let them try out the
ideas they have and see for themselves how certain cards and
strategies work against each other. V:TES is possibly the most
difficult CCG, and it takes a while to develop a solid familiarity
with the cards and strategies. Demonstrating these concepts only goes
so far for new players, and it takes a lot of learning by doing to get
the hang of things.

- Ben Peal, Prince of Boston
fu...@mindstorm.com

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Matt wrote:
>>Peter depicts anyone with a deck concept that doesn't fit his mold of
play as a little kid who will stomp his feet and get mad when his 7
card combat combo or 12 Werewolf packs don't come out.>>

Where do I do any such thing? The trouble I was highlighting with that example
is when folks go into a game with wildly different perceptions of what the
purpose of the game is--if player A is playing to maximize VPs, and player B is
playing to pull off a funny new card combo, with no mind towards VPs or
survival, neither player is going to have a good time.

>>I depict players with decks like Peter advocates as imaginationless
cheeze-weasels who must win at any cost to validate themselves rather
than just play a damn GAME.>>

And when have I said at any point that I (or anyone) must win at any cost to
validate myself rather than just play a damn game? Nowhere. In fact, I was
rather clear about how I play to win, but am actually rather unconcerned about
whether or not I actually do.

>>So, if we can both acknowledge that few people fit my depiction AND
few people fit his depiction then we're better off as a community>>

No one is not acknowledging that there are different play styles. There is a
problem, however, when play style A interacts with play style B, as the two
don't work well together, and no one has a good time. As "playing to win" is
far more definable and quantifyable than "playing for fun", it strikes me as
only prudent to assume that most people who are playing the game are "playing
to win", and when I sit down at a table with 4 other unknown players, to assume
that they are going to be playing effective decks that will do their very best
to kill me, so I will sit down with the same. Going into such a situation
assuming that the other players are going to be "playing for fun", whatever
that means, will doubtlessly result in most people having not such a good
time--some decks will be too good, and some will be useless.

>>(Derek wrote:) Winning itself is nice, butI prefer to have fun when I play...

and ah,
the thrill of winning with something that ISN'T the tried-and-true
formula. Or just the thrill of realizing that your deck may not have
won, but represented an important advance in the search for HOW to win - and
next time you'll be able to use it.>>

And again, I have never, ever, advocated "winning at any cost". I have
advocated playing the game to win, and consequently using effective decks, and
expecting other to do the same. If you can make an effective deck that is new
and exciting, more power to you.

>>Prior to last year, the Jyhad community rewarded both aspects via peer
approval. I won quite a few big tourneys "in my day" and what made the
wins special is the 18-20 people who shook my hand after each table
and said "Thats a really neat deck. Good luck at the next table. Can I
see the whole deck when you are done?">>

Which is great, but A) where does the "prior to last year" have anything to do
with this and B) why can't people shake your hand after each table when you win
with *any* deck, rather than a clever, unseen angle deck?

>>I gain no joy from seeing a player with 22 S:CE cards. I gain no joy
from seeing a person with 22 stealth cards and 22 bleed modifiers.>>

Why not? Why does it matter what cards your opponent is using? Either they have
a good deck, or they don't. Why does it matter if there are 34 different cards
by name in the deck rather than 12? Does seeing a Bonding this time and a
Conditioning next time really make the game more interesting than seeing a
Conditioning both times?

>>I gain no joy because these people have decided to throw away a whole
aspect of the game (the deck construction portion) by using a cookie
cutter deck.>>

What exactly is a "cookie cutter" deck? And how does using a lot of a given
card result in throwing away the deck construction aspect of the game? Using my
22 S:CE deck as an example (as it is a pretty extreme one), the deck in
question (an all Protean bleed deck, with light permanent intercept, lots of
untap, copious pool gain, Garous and Meat Hooks) seems unlikely to fit anyone's
"cookie cutter", and has been slowly evolving for literally years--every time I
play it, I adjust ratios, swap new cards in and out, tweak the crypt, whatever.
It has 22 S:CE cards because that is the best number for the deck--it has
enough to work, but not too many that it hand jams on them (some are offensive
S:CE, some are for use when blocking). How is this a "cookie cutter" deck? I'm
not taking this as a personal affront or anything, but you seem to be throwing
around an awful lot of misconceptions.

>>And yes Robert, I believe that these decks are infinitely easier to
build than the more creative decks that I have used and have had used
against me.>>

I'd debate that point. There is nothing "easy" about building a deck with a lot
of a single card--how many is too many? How often do you need to draw such a
card? How do you avoid gumming up your hand? Yeah, it is easy to build certain
deck designs (Malk S+B for instance) by throwing together a handfull of the
appropriate cards--you are bound to get some sort of sucess out of it, but it
is very difficult to build *any* deck that will do consistiently well against a
varied and well evolved field of opposition.

>>I am going to continue to laud the people like Derek who choose to win
with creativity and style, and I am going to continue to feel decks
like the ones Peter advocates>>

And what kind of decks are those? I advocate using decks that can win. Some
decks that can win are single minded and focused, doing only one thing over and
over (if their prey can't deal with this one thing, they win, but if their prey
can, they lose...); some decks that can win are all over the place, do a lot of
everything, and do it in varied ways. How is one of these any *better* on an
absolute sense than the other? I'm not looking for everyone to play Weenie
Dom/Misdirect Bleed decks, but I am looking for everyone to play effective
decks that can win, and not have people say "Fuck you" because I chose to play
an effective deck at ina given game.

>>kills a bit of the spirit of the game, because every new player than emulates
the cookie-cutter winner is another person who will ignore the first aspect of
Jyhad.>>

The "sprit of the game" What is that, exactly? Might I find the defenition in
the same book as the one for "cheesy"? "The spirit of the game" is a completely
subjective concept, and you can't expect that others will think the same thing
you do. My idea of what is "the spirit of the game" is clearly different than
yours, which is fine, but what is my idea of "the spirit of the game" is is
supported by the rule book, and thus, if someone assumes that I am playing the
game as per the instructions in the rule book, they are likely to be correct.
It is unlikely that anyone could guess as to what your idea of "the spirit of
the game" is on a blind meeting, and consequently can't live up to your ideas
without knowing what your ideas are.

>>Don't give up on style. Please please please.>>

And I have never advocated giving up on style. As long as the style makes for
an effective deck.

When I sit down to play a game of VTES, I do so because I enjoy playing games
and I enjoy hanging out with my friends. I play with effective decks, and hope
my friends/opponents do the same thing. As a player, it is my responsibility to
be pleasant to play with, entertaining, considerate, and good natured (just
like in all other areas of social life), and so I am, and hope my opponents act
in kind. It is not, however, my responsibility to build my decks such that they
fit other people's ambigiously defined defenition of "fun" or "uncheesy". I
build my decks such that they can win VPs, as that is why I am playing a CCG,
rather than an RPG, where there are no well defined victory conditions, and
hope that my opponents are doing the same, as that way we all have a good time,
and no one gets miffed because their poorly defined idea of "fun decks" weren't
adhered to.

Messages.Author: Ian Lee
Messages.Body:
>One might think Malkavian S+B right off the bat, but I would
>challenge someone to make a really good Malk S+B deck that can consistiently
>win, in the hands of a bad player, in a well developed play environment (i.e.
>an environment where the deck is just as likely to run into, for example, a
>strong intercept deck, a bounce deck, a speedy bleed deck, a rush deck, or a
>rampant pool gain deck).

Does a well developed play environment consist of only tournament level decks
or, at least, a highly competitive mentality?

I've played with about 4 different groups since I started playing. None
consistently played tournament decks. Some decks just rip apart such
environments regardless as to who plays them. While it may seem stupid not to
put answers in decks, there's a point where you aren't building the decks that
interest you but are building metagame decks just so you can compete. That can
be a turn off for a lot of the casual players I've played with.

On a more general CCG level, CCGers need to play against people of like mind
(to some extent, anyway), echoing what you said in the initial post. If people
want to screw around rather than try to win, that can be okay if everyone is of
that mind. Similarly, if people want to test their tournament decks until they
are perfectly tuned, that works when the others are doing the same thing. My
preference is somewhere in the middle, where people try to get rogue decks
(which may be awful or may be the next big tournament play, though it isn't
possible to know that playing just in a casual environment) to work.

>> I think he was only talking about the extreme player who wants to show

>
>And I'm only talking about the extreme player that puts 22 Majesties in his
>deck. I'm just trying to prevent this player from becoming more common than
>he already is, and seeing James advocate this action is what set me off.

You can't prevent it, though. You can only provide a counterexample,
and hope that players will follow -that-. (though I appreciate the
kudos and quoth-tations and such =)

The inherent problem is that it's just lots easier to put bunches of
the same card in your deck. New players tend to do this sort of
reflexively, without realizing what they're doing to THEMSELVES. And
if they're in a playgroup which is ALSO relatively new, then they
probably tend to win more, as people haven't learned how to deal with
stuff like that yet.

About the only thing you can really do is to teach people how to deal
with extreme focus. Sometimes extreme focus is necessary - a Tremere
combat deck, for example, NEEDS to have a whole bunch of Theft of
Vitae in it. The way you go about the REST of the combat is up to
you, but including 10-12 Theft of Vitae is probably best-guess in any
given environment.

But to deal with extreme focus, the trick is to recognize the focus
and STOP playing into its hand. If a deck wants to move its stealth,
quit blocking it. If a deck has tons of intercept, stop taking +1
stealth and/or undirected actions, and just bleed for awhile.

>I play very focused decks (except my old Tremere deck that was a utility
>monster!) but I do it with only 6 copies of a particular card (once I built
>a deck with 10 Flashes in it because it needed long range and a second
>round. I felt dirty but did it)

Can't support any sort of card limit, voluntary or otherwise. Some
cards need to be in more than multiples of just 6, or just 8, etc....
or your deck DOES defocus itself. You mention a Weather Control deck,
but with only 6 WCs in the deck, WC was undoubtedly a feature of only
half the combats in your games. See the contradiction? =/

As you say yourself, you need long range and a 2nd round EVERY time;
that means ten Flashes, or you won't be getting it every time.
(THA/CEL by any chance?) This doesn't make the deck any less
creative, it's just that it's reaching towards a "corner case"
scenario a little. Sometimes that leaves only one solution.

>True, but I'm not gonna stop trying to inspire people to be more creative,
>and I cannot stop feeling like a part of the game dies when at the end of a
>round I see 22 Majesties in someone's graveyard.

22 Majesties is a great way to get handjammed. It generally provides
its own counter -- if you suspect such a thing exists, then decide
early on to either block everything (run them out of Majesty), or
block nothing (let them bleed for 1 with 7 Majesty in hand).

Of course, (evil grin), if you include "information" cards such as
Tortured Confession, Owl Companion, or Scrying of Secrets, you can
learn quickly what someone's deck is likely to look like. If their
hand has 1 Master, 2 bleed cards, and 4 Majesties, you have adequate
information to immediately assume the "grit your teeth and block
nothing" stance, unless you -can- block everything. The
rush-forward-and-Majesty style falls over to a deck that is willing to
leave a bunch of minions untapped and sit patiently.

>Sure. Something like that. I don't like any tactic that requires so many
>copies of one card. Its sad and removes deck slots from being dedicated to
>creative strategies. 12 Grapples does not foil 22 Majesties.

"creative" and "bunch of different cards" don't mean the same thing,
however. There are perfectly creative strategies that rely on 10-ish
of a certain card - a Ravnos Trick of Danya/Cairo Int'l/Reality deck,
for example.

(idle note: 12 Grapples -does- foil 22 Majesties. Torporized
vampires cannot bleed or play Majesty, and each Grapple usually
results in a torporized vampire.)

Just because something has a ton of the same card in it doesn't make
it uncreative. If, for example, I decide to make the Spawning Pool
deck, I'm going to need a whole BUNCH of Rat's Warning cards.
Probably about 12, because that's the most card-efficient, and I can
spend the rest of my card slots on toys such as Raven Spies, Owl
Companions, or whatever else might seem appropriate for a Nossie
intercept deck. Or I could just use the Spawning Pool angle as a
"threat" if anyone tries to press, and use Guard Dogs/Carrion
Crows/Sewer Lids for the first round. =)

Hm. That sounds amusing. I may try that soon. =)

-- Derek

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
sv...@chartermi.net (Matt Latham) wrote in message news:<978c2422.01062...@posting.google.com>...

> First, lets clear up some perception issues. Both Peter's Camp (which
> includes the chairman of VEKN, which pretty much means people like me
> have no place in the NWO of VEKN tourney Jyhad. Makes me sad)

The NWO? I don't mean to be inflammatory, but what is a tourney
if not a series of games that are all about winning? Has that
not always been the definition of a tournament? If you don't
like playing VTES in a playing-to-win environment, why would you
ever want to play in a tournament? Why not just play the "fun
creative" kind of games in a less-structured format?

> CCG's have two parts to their game: Deck construction and Play Skill.
> Magic, as a game, no longer rewards the first aspect. Players get
> their decks off the Net as generated by a handful of players and use
> them at tourneys. The winner at the end of the day is the one who had
> the best matchups and for the most part showed the best Play skill

I suspect that, to the extent that it's true, this is a result of
the maturing of each particular CCG environment. As more and more
people play a game, more and more useful strategies/cards/etc are
discovered, and via the Internet this knowledge is easily distributed
worldwide. Basically, it becomes much easier to learn how to make
(or "copy") a good deck than to learn how to play the game especially
well.

> And yes Robert, I believe that these decks are infinitely easier to
> build than the more creative decks that I have used and have had used
> against me.
>
> I am going to continue to laud the people like Derek who choose to win
> with creativity and style, and I am going to continue to feel decks
> like the ones Peter advocates kills a bit of the spirit of the game,
> because every new player than emulates the cookie-cutter winner is
> another person who will ignore the first aspect of Jyhad.
>
> Don't give up on style. Please please please.

This is all very well, but as time goes by, it becomes possible for
*every* deck concept to seem noncreative and boring because everybody's
seen them all before.

Why not just accept that, to a new player, all the decks in the world
are new and interesting, and be happy that they think so? It doesn't
hurt anyone for you to play with "new" combos that you think are
especially clever; nor does it hurt anyone for those who like the "old"
combos to use them.

It really is all relative, you know. At the Northeast Regionals I
met Remy from Quebec playing a deck that intended to put Fortitude
skill cards on other people's vampires, then Mind Rape them, Rave all
but one of their blood off, and Force of Will/Daring the Dawn to bleed
unblockably and burn them. To someone who's never thought of this,
it's a brilliant and hilarious combo. But I remembered having read
about the concept a few months back on the newsgroup (Noal was talking
about a possibly-somewhat-different variant on it, I think), and so
although I thought it was kinda cool that he'd actually built and played
such a deck, I wasn't especially amazed by his creativity. (I certainly
don't intend that as a slam. My deck was a very predictable Tzimisce
intercept-combat and Smiling Jack thing.)

Josh

Messages.Author: Matt Latham
Messages.Body:
Hey, at least in one post I got your name right...

You ask me to define "spirit of the game". The fact that you wrote this
thread to begin with shows that there is a difference in belief, and that
there are numbers of players in both camps.

Jyhad was made just after Magic as a game to appeal to those whom Magic may
not appeal to. (This from a discussion I had with a guy in WotC) It has a
group atmosphere, longer games, and, via politics, almost required
socialization. "Back in the Day", tournaments were more an extension of your
Saturday Jyhad game, more designed for social interaction rather than
cutthroat competition. As I explained to Robert, the "before last year"
should have been "before last year in my experience".

Further definitions you asked for: A cookie cutter deck is an archetype that
is designed by one and copied by hundreds. I'm sure you could make your own
examples.

> And when have I said at any point that I (or anyone) must win at any cost
to
> validate myself rather than just play a damn game?

Exactly. Thats why I said it's unfair of me to do so.

<In fact, I was rather clear about how I play to win, but am actually rather

unconcerned aboutwhether or not I actually do.>

Hmm.. this surprises me. I take you as a "winning is very important to me"
kinda guy, which is not wrong or anything but the statement above clearly
shows I'm wrong. I apologize.

> No one is not acknowledging that there are different play styles. There is
a
> problem, however, when play style A interacts with play style B, as the
two
> don't work well together, and no one has a good time. As "playing to win"
is
> far more definable and quantifyable than "playing for fun",

I disagree. Your prey bounces a bleed to me. My pred has a stealth deck and
my prey bouncing me such that I haven't been able to get into combat. In
combat with you I chuck sewer lids, press, and toss a car, because I have to
clear my hand jam. I know few "focused winning" types that wouldn't call me
an asshole for sending your minion to hell, but I've got to clear my hand to
get some rush or intercept to deal with Stealth Pred, or a Divine
Intervention to get around Bouncy Prey. Your line is only slightly clearer
than mine.

<<B) why can't people shake your hand after each table when you winwith
*any* deck, rather than a clever, unseen angle deck?>>

Because the person with the cookie cutter played you in one aspect of the
game.. the person who beat you with a creative deck beat you in both
aspects, and showed you the respect to dig around his vast collection for
something new. (I know, you'll say that bringing a focused winning deck
regardless of the creativity involved is showing respect to your opponents.
I agree to disagree on this.)

> >>I gain no joy from seeing a player with 22 S:CE cards. I gain no joy
> from seeing a person with 22 stealth cards and 22 bleed modifiers.>>
>
> Why not? Why does it matter what cards your opponent is using? Either they
have
> a good deck, or they don't.

Good to you is VP gaining. Good to me is different or clever. I agreed to
disagree with Robert on this one. The crux of your issue is that my criteria
of "good" is arbitrary and yours is "in the rules". If my criteria is so
subjective, why are viewpoints like mine universal enough to warrant your
original post? Why does the stigma exist?

You acknowledge that you've been told "fuck you" on occasion? Why?

My feeling as to why is because those people love Jyhad as a game because it
has the potential to be different than most other games. Anyone can "win"
any game. Jyhad allows one to "win with style" like Derek suggests, using
different angles and different ideas, not just the cookie cutters that are
"tried and true".

Thats my opinion.

This thread has convinced me that I am a snob, and that if I am going to
play in tourneys nowadays that I best prepare for both people who believe in
my win condition and people who don't. Further, its mean and rude of me to
apply peer pressure in public to people who believe in your Jyhad, so I
won't.

If thats what you were going for, you win.

Matt

verbaitim from a deck listing)--it is going to have different card ratios,
different defenses, different offenses. Yes, on a basic level, every Malk S+B
deck is going to win by bleeding at stealth, but other than that, they are all
going to be different.

>>Hmm.. this surprises me. I take you as a "winning is very important to me"
kinda guy, which is not wrong or anything but the statement above clearly

Again, quite all right. That you are assuming that I am a "winning is very
important to me" kind of guy enlightens my understanding of your world view,
however.

>>I disagree. Your prey bounces a bleed to me. My pred has a stealth deck and
my prey bouncing me such that I haven't been able to get into combat. In
combat with you I chuck sewer lids, press, and toss a car, because I have to

Intervention to get around Bouncy Prey. Your line is only slightly clearer
than mine.>>

What I meant is that if I sit down with a well designed deck that is very
effective at getting VPs, and you are my prey, and your deck is very good at
getting out Giovanni Allies, and not much else, neither of us are going to have
a good time--I'm not going to have a good time, 'cause you are going to provide
no challenge. You are not going to have a good time because you are going to be
steamrollered by a "cheesy" deck.

>>Because the person with the cookie cutter played you in one aspect of the
game.. the person who beat you with a creative deck beat you in both
aspects, and showed you the respect to dig around his vast collection for
something new. (I know, you'll say that bringing a focused winning deck
regardless of the creativity involved is showing respect to your opponents.
I agree to disagree on this.)>>

For one, as I mentioned before, I have no need to see my opponents using new
deck designs. Sure, when I see a clever new deck, I'm amused, but I'm not
offended when my opponents play old standards. I'm no more impressed when
someone kills me with something new than when they kill me with something old.
A deck is a deck, and I'm happy to be playing, regardless.

>>Good to you is VP gaining. Good to me is different or clever. I agreed to
disagree with Robert on this one. The crux of your issue is that my criteria
of "good" is arbitrary and yours is "in the rules".>>

Precisely. How can you expect other people to play according to your arbitrary
criteria of what is good? You are setting yourself up to be disapointed in
every game. At least with a well defined criteria (i.e. play by the rules), it
is easier to expect that people live up to your hopes.

>>If my criteria is so subjective, why are viewpoints like mine universal
enough to warrant your original post?>>

Because lots of people hold a similar subjective view, and many of them seem to
get upset when their arbitrary view of how to play VTES is not adhered to. And
then they show up around here and malign people for playing "cheesy" decks. I
just find it interesting.

>>Why does the stigma exist?>>

What stigma is that?

>>You acknowledge that you've been told "fuck you" on occasion? Why?>>

The only time I can recall is at a large tournament at Origins one year, I sat
down with my Nosferatu Rush deck, and my prey was a Malkavian S+B deck. I
torporized every vampire he brough out before it took a single action (as he
had exactly zero combat defense), and after killing 4 or 5 of his vampires, he
picked up his stuff, quit the game, and flipped me the bird (he never actually
said "Fuck You"). I wasn't rude, unsportsman like, or in any way pricky. I just
played the game according to the rules, and my opponent was unhappy with how it
turned out.

>>My feeling as to why is because those people love Jyhad as a game because it
has the potential to be different than most other games. Anyone can "win"
any game. Jyhad allows one to "win with style" like Derek suggests, using
different angles and different ideas, not just the cookie cutters that are
"tried and true".>>

Yes you can win with style, but as there is no way to quantify what "style" is,
there is no way to expect that everyone will live up to your expectations. I
figure that if my expectation is little more than that my opponents will play
by the rules and try to win, I am less likely to be disapointed.

>>This thread has convinced me that I am a snob, and that if I am going to
play in tourneys nowadays that I best prepare for both people who believe in
my win condition and people who don't.>>

I'm not quite sure why one would go to a tournament (where the default purpose
is to try and win, otherwise why have a tournament?) and expect that people
will be not playing to win.

>>Further, its mean and rude of me to apply peer pressure in public to people
who believe in your Jyhad, so I won't.

If thats what you were going for, you win.>>

If me winning means that less people are going to be berated for playing the
game by the rules, then yaaa!



extra deck space that can be used for cards to win the
game, where the poor Grapple deck, after his
12 Grapples, has to pack another 10 undead strengths
and then 5 disarms. Soon that deck hasn't any space
for anything beyond combat, so it's stuck being a rush
deck, while the Majesty deck has probably 10 more slots
that would be combat slots if S:CE weren's so degenrate
that can be used for actions, modifiers, stealth, intercept,
or whatever it needs to accomplish other goals. And let's
not even consider that the Grapple deck has to have at least
a 2, and probably a 3 card combo in hand to be able to make
the Majesty player pay for his one card combat solution.

So when it comes right down to it, the only way for a
deck to beat S:CE without being a pure combat deck
is to block and hope for no Majesty, while keeping a
devastating strike in reserve, or strike and hope for
no Majesty, keeping the Wolf's Claws for use after
you're sure there's no S:CE. That's pretty poor.

And I don't even want to get into the extra actions
or blocks that Majesty allows at superior. I really
believe that S:CE untap this vampire (or continue
at +1 stealth) is the most degenerate one card combo
in the game (except maybe Grave Robbing), and to have
the rulings that help it along is really frustrating.

- Jason Bell

I agree. Lobby for the end of S:CE beats first strike,

To get another sense of how sad the situation is currently,

blood or free. Not sure about discipline, though. If it's
1 blood, there should be no discipline, I figure.

almost certainly not readily available to clans that are *already*
really good at combat. I wouldn't have been unhappy to see an Assamite
anti-S:CE card, but I'm satisfied with the current state.

Anyway, I digress.

>Because Majesty (does anybody else always spell that with

>game, where the poor Grapple deck, after his

If you're not planning to fight, why are you trying to catch
them? A deck with 12 Grapples and nothing else in the way
of combat is a misdesign, as you're better off pitching the
Grapples for something useful. Grapple is a support card; it
does nothing useful in and of itself, in terms of torping
vampires. It gets you a strength-damage handpoke and maybe
a press at superior.

And if you're not a fighty deck, why worry about Majesty
at all? You're not trying to beat anyone's head in, you're
trying to do whatever it is your deck does (intercept/
runaway, vote, bleed, corrupt, whatever). Majesty isn't frustrating
to you under these circumstances because of SCE, it's
frustrating because of the untap (also available with
Earth Meld yarra yarra), which sets up extra actions or
extra blocks.

>And let's
>not even consider that the Grapple deck has to have at least
>a 2, and probably a 3 card combo in hand to be able to make
>the Majesty player pay for his one card combat solution.

Not a problem, as the Grapple deck is a fighty rush deck,
so it has 90 cards worth of space for its combat solution,
whereas the Majesty deck has 10-20 cards of deckspace
for its own combat solution.

>So when it comes right down to it, the only way for a
>deck to beat S:CE without being a pure combat deck
>is to block and hope for no Majesty, while keeping a
>devastating strike in reserve, or strike and hope for
>no Majesty, keeping the Wolf's Claws for use after
>you're sure there's no S:CE. That's pretty poor.

Or you could just oust it. Decks don't 'beat' SCE.
Decks oust players. The only deck SCE stops from
gaining VP is a combat deck. Grapples go in combat
decks. Grapples stop SCE.

A bleed or vote deck couldn't give a good shit
about SCE (again, the untaps could be a problem,
but SCE isn't), because they aren't looking to get
into a fight in the first place.

Bleedy decks, of course, can use Thoughts Betrayed
(dom:malks, lasombra, ventrue) or The Jones
(ser:followers of set) to hose SCE if they find
it truly obnoxious -- but they're more likely
to find SCE a relief, as it means their vampire
won't get beaten up.

Yah, there's bruise, but bruise decks will act
as combat decks (bringing cards that hose SCE),
and have their own card-balance issues (drawing
bleed when they want fight and vice versa).

>And I don't even want to get into the extra actions
>or blocks that Majesty allows at superior. I really
>believe that S:CE untap this vampire (or continue
>at +1 stealth) is the most degenerate one card combo
>in the game (except maybe Grave Robbing), and to have
>the rulings that help it along is really frustrating.

Oh come on. You hardly ever see Graverobbing played,
because it isn't a freaking one-card combo. It kind
of requires a torporized vampire and stealth. Who
has dominate and stealth? Malks, who can't fight,
and Lasombra, who can. Once Lasombra assault-and-robbery
decks start dominating the tourney scene, I'll start
to fret about Graverobbing, but excuse me for not
breaking into a cold sweat just now.

Also, there haven't _been_ any rulings that increase
Majesty's power, or the power of SCE in general.
It works as it always has.

gomi

Just as an example. I have no desire to quash creativity in any way, shape, or
form. I just also have no desire to quash competition in the name of
creativity. Calling people "cheesy" for using decks that are too effective, or
calling their decks degenerate in a vain attempt to get them to make decks more
to *my* liking accomplishes nothing but pissing people off. I'd much rather be
graciously killed by a deck I was unprepared for than go off saying "if he
wasn't playing such a cheesy deck, he wouldn't have got me..."

enlightens me

other

original posting? I realize you cannot speak definitively on this as it's

Why do I think people are offended by "cheesy" decks? There are plently of
reasons. They don't understand the game enough to see that there are ways to
combat such decks, and that they are self regulating. They think that seeing
the same card over and over again is boring. They are sick of their "fun" decks
getting killed before they get to do anything. They think that card limits make
the game a better place without realizing that card limits make certain deck
strategies overly powerful and other deck strategies unplayable, and attempt to
use peer pressure to fix the problems caused, rather than simply playing by the
rules the game was designed for. I'm not saying that you fit under any of these
categories necessarily, but they are reasons I have come across that result in
the "cheezy" stigma.

And this goes back to what is degenerate and what is uncreative? You clearly
have a defenition for these words in your mind, and don't like it when people
fulfil these defenitions. I don't believe in a "degenerate" deck, and I find

designed deck, regardless of what it does, they are, in my mind, playing to win

Interestingly, even my bruise/bleed decks aren't too frightened about
someone packing Majesty. Since I normally design them in the form of
"bleed for 1, block? no? modifier for 3...", I'm not wasting any of
my precious bleed when they block and Majesty. All I'm doing is

players, I have to say. They WILL run out. Even a PRE weenie horde
will run out. It's not that they'll run out in their deck, it's that
they'll run out in their HAND. Majesty is a standalone trick. Every
combat, to a Majesty deck, is a one-card affair. As a result, they
don't get to move any cards, and if they only have one Majesty in
hand, they have a less-than-50% chance of drawing up another Majesty.

Everyone hear me out there? LESS than 50%. If you have 22 Majesties
in a 90-card deck, and you have one in your hand, the chances of you
drawing up another one are 21/83. That's approximately 25%. Even in
a 60-card deck, it's still only 21/53... which is still only 39.6%.
If you could find a roulette wheel in Vegas where your odds of winning
were 60.4% on every spin, you would have to be pried away from it with
a crowbar, wouldn't you?

If you have 10 Majesties in a 90-card deck, and you have one in your
hand, the chances go down to 9/83, which is pretty damn small. If you
put such a deck in a situation where it needs to play 3 per turn, then
you WILL, eventually, catch them... and it WILL happen sooner than you
think.

-- Derek

Consider this hypothetical situation:

We're back at Jyhad, nothing else EXCEPT bleed is doing exceptionally
well, because the designers didn't think about putting bleed bounce in.
So, we're now printing a hypothetical V:TES.

We decide to put a bleed bounce type card in for it. Here it is:

Bleed Bounce
Master: Out-Of-Turn
2 pool
Play this card when a minion is bleeding you. Tap an untapped vampire
you control with a capacity above four. That minion is now bleeding a
Methuselah of your choice (which may not be you or its controller).

Now, we'd still have over-powered bleed, but citing Bleed Bounce
regarding it wouldn't be the best thing to do. Bleed would be
over-powered, but Bleed Bounce would be underpowered.

In the current situation, that's basically what we have. Assume that
S:CE is too powerful. (People can argue about that, of course, but
let's just assume it.) Dog Pack is *under*powered. Dog Pack, were LSJ
and the current Design Team writing it *today*, might read:

Dog Pack
Retainer
2 blood
Requires Gangrel
Any minion in combat with the Gangrel with this retainer may not use
"combat ends" as a strike.

Were we re-writing Jyhad from the ground up today, I think many of us
would tend towards the suggestion that a number of people (I think Peter
was the first one I recall seriously mentioning it, way back in the
mists of time) have made, making it round ends.

But Dog Pack is just weak. It being weak doesn't prove anything about
S:CE. It just proves designers make mistakes.

[specious math argument deleted]

> If you have 10 Majesties in a 90-card deck, and you have one in your
> hand, the chances go down to 9/83, which is pretty damn small. If you
> put such a deck in a situation where it needs to play 3 per turn, then

Of course, 3 per turn is a best case scenario. Only on defense can
you get cards out of their hand at that rate. If they block, they
get to look at your strike, then decide whether their dwindling
supply of S:CE is worth the use.

Also, the reason your otherwise sound math argument is not
quite spot on is that the Majesty deck will be cycling cards
at a normal rate, so that 25% chance to refresh into one
increases rapidly as other cards are played, like masters,
intercept, discard phase, what have you.

Finally, it's hard to understate the importance of table
dynamics in the presence of Majesty as well. If the table
is light on Grapples (or the other few S:CE foils), it
doesn't matter if the Majesty player is overdogging,
as the combat decks do not want to waste cross-table
actions on something that most likely won't even tap
the problem minion. Don't believe it doesn't happen,
I've been on both sides of it, with my FoS deck that
no one would step in front of and my buddy's prince
deck that no one would help out against. Mid-game
actions need tangible results, and getting the next
Majesty out of a player's hand is a tough sell.

All I'm saying is that S:CE is a 12-20 card combat
solution, that has far fewer downsides than almost
any other combat strategy (Grapple costs 40 cards,
weapons cost a lot of pool and actions to put into
play, consistent agg damage requires Gangrel,
Thoughts Betrayed costs 2 off the vampire
before you even fight, yadda yadda yadda).

And when you also consider how few foils
there are to it compared to the other options
(maneuver out of Grapple, weapons can be
stolen or destroyed though not often,
Gangrel's agg can be stopped by casual Fortitude),
then you start to see how this is a problem:
A complete combat solution with a minimum of
foils for under 20 cards, with the enormous
untap advantage thrown in to boot.

And the solution is not a rare 2 pool retainer
for one clan only. That card's cost, rarity, and
effect show me clearly that the design team
doesn't see S:CE as the problem I think it is,
and that's discouraging.

- Jason Bell

actually move any of those cards (especially the intercept, since
you're taking a bunch of 0-stealth actions). As I stated above, he

Nobody was suggesting that you should attempt to recruit the entire
table to your side. I'm saying that you should be able to break
through a Majesty deck by sheer force of numbers, if you have enough
combat in your deck.

A deck with 22 Majesties is its own downside - what does it do when it
doesn't sit next to combat, or sits next to someone whose defense is
"Deflect, bloat, and ignore"?

>All I'm saying is that S:CE is a 12-20 card combat
>solution, that has far fewer downsides than almost

Nobody is saying that S:CE isn't good. However, I simply don't think
it's overpowered anymore, even Majesty. There is just too much combat
out there in the game, and people are beginning to realize that the
idea of "combat defense" is silly on the face of it; it's more worth
your time to put in some cards that allow you to hit back.

The more people in a game that are trying to hit you, the less useful
S:CE becomes.

>And when you also consider how few foils
>there are to it compared to the other options
>(maneuver out of Grapple, weapons can be
>stolen or destroyed though not often,
>Gangrel's agg can be stopped by casual Fortitude),
>then you start to see how this is a problem:
>A complete combat solution with a minimum of
>foils for under 20 cards, with the enormous
>untap advantage thrown in to boot.

Complete combat solution EXCEPT for when you sit next to the Grapple
deck. Or when you sit next to the Tzimisce intercept deck. Or when
you sit next to the Animalism untap wall. Or when you have the
Protean weenie-poke-horde behind you. Or when you have the Tremere
chucking around Thoughts Betrayed. Or when you sit behind the deck
that just Deflects all your bleeds, plays Minion Tap/5th, and ignores
you completely.

Majesty comes with its own risks. Relying on it, and it alone in a
deck will work sometimes, and get you very dead other times. Again,
sheer weight of numbers is frequently enough to handle the problem.

Not to mention that the untap advantage is nice, but hardly
overpowering. So you bleed me for 3, I block you, and you untap. Now
what are you going to do? You can't bleed again. If you're the
Ventrue, you can call a vote, but now your deck is RELYING on having
all its bleed actions blocked so you can cycle the Majesties and get
to your vote cards. What will you do if the vote gets blocked? You
won't be able to play any of your vote cards. What will you do if
someone just ignores the bleed action, or Deflects it? You'll be
stuck with a bunch of votes in hand.

>And the solution is not a rare 2 pool retainer
>for one clan only. That card's cost, rarity, and
>effect show me clearly that the design team
>doesn't see S:CE as the problem I think it is,
>and that's discouraging.

This paragraph shows me clearly that you don't understand the current
state of the game all too well. That's also discouraging.

Dog Pack was printed in Ancient Hearts, several years ago. This is
also the set that gave us Return to Innocence, so there's no question
that the design team for AH was smoking crack at least part of the
time.

But what makes you think that the design team for AH bears even the
remotest relation to the current design team?

And what decks are you so worried about that aren't getting their fair
shake against S:CE? The reason weapons are so hard to use isn't S:CE;
it's that they cost pool and an action, and the action is
interceptable. Big emphasis on "the action is interceptable".

-- Derek

You are totally, TOTALLY missing the point. Trap/CC/Song is an
extremely powerful combo. All the cards are free. All the cards can
be cycled easily (playable before range). It hoses Dodge. It hoses
most "poke-for-1" agg decks. It hoses Fortitude (can't prevent Crows
with Skin of Steel). It will make most combat decks pay for entering
combat at all, and with the Aid from Bats, it's entirely possible to
escape unscathed by pressing to end, if you need.

If S:CE didn't exist, Trap/CC/Song would be ridiculously overpowered.
As it stands now, S:CE provides a welcome alternative to including
enough ranged combat to hit back at a Trap/CC/Song deck, or to
including enough maneuvers to catch them and THEN hit them back.

the time, and S:CE should win 50% of the time, NOT that combat should
win 100% of the time.

They won't be cycling cards in combat--if they have 1 Majesty in their hand
when you get in a fight on a given turn, and they play it, they are unlikely to
draw a second from the single card they play (the Majesty).

>>All I'm saying is that S:CE is a 12-20 card combat
solution, that has far fewer downsides than almost
any other combat strategy (Grapple costs 40 cards,
weapons cost a lot of pool and actions to put into
play, consistent agg damage requires Gangrel,
Thoughts Betrayed costs 2 off the vampire
before you even fight, yadda yadda yadda).>>

No one is debating that S:CE is incredibly efficient, and possibly overpowered.
If that is your angle, then yes, you are correct. However, as I mentioned
elsewhere, if you are playing a deck that cares if your opponent plays a
Majesty, you play with ways to foil the Majesty. Otherwise, you don't care. The
only decks that really care if their opponent plays a Majesty is a Rush deck
(as pretty much every attack you make needs to result in a dead vampire, or you
will fail), and they are good at foiling Majesty (IG, TB, Psyche, Dog Pack,
whatever)--otherwise they aren't going to work anyway. Any other deck just
isn't going to care if you Majesty--you block someone (or they block you), you
attempt to punch them for 1, they Majesty. The end result is that you are up
one blood--you weren't going to be doing much damage to them anyways, so how
does it matter if they play the Majesty?

>>And when you also consider how few foils
there are to it compared to the other options
(maneuver out of Grapple, weapons can be
stolen or destroyed though not often,
Gangrel's agg can be stopped by casual Fortitude),
then you start to see how this is a problem:
A complete combat solution with a minimum of
foils for under 20 cards, with the enormous
untap advantage thrown in to boot.>>

But it isn't even close to a complete combat solution--decks that plan on
gaining an advantage from killing things *need* to have S:CE foils inherrent in
their design. Against such a deck, someone with 20 Majesties is still going to
be killed. On the other hand, if you aren't using S:CE foils, then you should
expect that your opponent will play S:CE, and thus not care about combat. When
I play my Rush deck, I hope, no, pray that my opponents will be playing decks
that have 20 Majesties in them. That is because it is a dedicated combat deck
that laughs at Majesty. On the other hand, when I play my Protean bleed deck, I
still hope that my opponent is playing with 20 Majesties 'cause, well, I just
don't care--I have no interest in fighting them anyways.

I agree that the entire combat environment in VTES is, pretty much, either
"play S:CE, or play anti S:CE", but that is what we have until something
changes it (and I'd be happy if something did, but until then, this is what
we've got). In such an environment, half assed combat simply isn't worth
playing--if you can't deal with S:CE, don't commit much deck space to combat
offense, as you will be asking to be screwed. For instance, if you are playing,
say, a Gangrel wall deck, if you aren't going to be using multiple Dog packs,
it would be foolish to include more than a handfull of Bone Spurs. Sure,
sometimes you'll get to poke someone in the eye, but often your opponent will
just play S:CE. As this is going to happen, don't build your deck such that it
you will spend a great deal of time saying "Man. If only they hadn't played
that Majesty. Now my hand is gummed up..."

ruling, but it also seriously increased the power of Tremere combat? Or

Messages.Author: TigToad
Messages.Body:
> Sure, S:CE got more powerful - but lots of other changes happened too.
>
> You are taking one aspect of a number of complex changes, failing to
> take into account the intricacies of the situation, focusing on the one
> facet that supports your argument.

The bottom line is, IMO this is the best balanced CCG out there. S:CE
is very powerful for a number of reasons... and it can be beat in a
number of ways. (Who can win a game by only avoiding combat?) The best
part of this game is, to me, that any strategy from stealth bleed, to
weenie vote to rush combat can be destroyed by another kind of deck on
another table. This is the reason why a deck that sweeps a table one
night might be the first ousted the next...

If there is a deck type or card or way of playing that is winning in
your play group very consistantly...build a deck that destroys that deck
type (and hopefully has a good chance of winning in its own right!).
Minion Tap/Fifth getting you down? Play some light intercept...stealth
bleed a problem, throw some bounces in... S:CE bugging you? Play
stealth or immortal grapple combat types.

There are good ways around any card. The more effective those ways are,
(bleed bounce is very effective whereas Immortal Grapple combat is only
minorly effective as its a less desirable deck type), the better the
response is provided within the game. Really, I don't get upset when
someone plays a majesty... what are they really accomplishing? They are
hurting my minion as little as I am hurting theirs. Often, they spend a
blood to untap and I did more to them then they did to me.

Anyway, to make a roundabout argument and drawn out point, the more
broken a card or combination appears to be, from my experience, is more
often a result of the local metagame then it is an effective of a
certain type of card.

Off the soapbox.

Tig

Messages.Author: Derek Ray

On 24 Jun 2001 17:58:08 GMT, cur...@aol.com (Ian Lee) wrote:

>>Again, simply put - combat is balanced with S:CE when each wins 50% of
>>the time. And if you intend to overwhelm someone with combat, then

>
>What I'm getting out of this discussion is that the only worthwhile combat is
>combat that can deal with S:CE due to the prevalence of S:CE. Isn't this a bad
>thing?

If you intend to build a deck that wins by killing everything in its
path, you had better allow for S:CE in some fashion. And when you get
right down to it, S:CE doesn't do enough to stop this sort of deck; if
someone wants to get you, they'll get you. But whether or not they
can oust anyone after they get you is the trick.

If you intend to build a deck that wins by bleeding (or voting) and
killing anything that blocks it, then S:CE could well be a problem for
you. However, usually it works out that you've traded off your
ability to beat up ANYTHING for the ability to bleed. You open
yourself up to Deflection and S:CE, but you also have a lot more
potential and probably haven't hurt yourself much against other
combat.

If you intend to build a deck that uses light combat as a deterrent,
then you don't care very much about S:CE. Your primary intent is to
keep your own guys from being beaten up or intercepted, and opposing
S:CE handles the first job admirably. You DO want to beat up
intercept decks, or at least make them pay for blocking, but
Intercept/S:CE decks are not terribly prevalent, due to their
difficulty in actually ousting anyone; intercept/combat is much more
effective and popular, even if it's light "plink" combat that wears
you down over time.

And of course, if you intend to build a deck with no combat defense
whatsoever, S:CE is a beautiful thing to see opposing you. You don't
even get punched for 1.

>Combat should be interesting. S:CE does nothing to make combat interesting. I

S:CE provides a vital balance in the game. Without it, some
strategies would become vastly overpowered.

>believe it is entirely possible that its absence would have beneficial metagame
>effects as players focus less on how to defeat a single combat strategy. It

Players would quit focussing on how to beat S:CE, and would begin
focussing on how to defeat whichever new "trump" combat strategy
emerged, though.

The Gangrel would be near-unstoppable with the simple PRO/FOR deck -
the only cards required would be Claws and a prevent card. Include
Drawing out the Beast and Scorpion Sting if you want people to REALLY
stay put. The Assamites would be almost as strong; their Celerity and
unpreventable damage cards would mow down minions left and right. The
Brujah could trim down their thug-decks significantly, as they no
longer would need to pack reams of IG and other cards.

Non-combat decks would totally cease to see play, as they would simply
become targets for the other combat decks, and the game would
degenerate into a card version of the WWF, with vampire body parts
flying everywhere.

Is this TRULY what you are looking for?

-- Derek
