Whoever happens to have the cards in hand at the time. But damn near
every other deck gets run over, as there's no longer any suitable
defense against the easy-to-use combat disciplines PRO, QUI, or POT.
Right now, what's slowing them down is that all three of these
disciplines require a good chunk of supporting cards to make them
viable against S:CE.

>>Non-combat decks would totally cease to see play, as they would simply

>would get back to trying to oust.

I repeat, non-combat decks would totally cease to see play, as they
would simply get run over by the combat decks that would be
everywhere. There was a time when weenie Misdirection was a feature
of every single tournament - you went into things KNOWING that you'd
see at least three/four weenie decks, and you knew that if you didn't
plan to deal with it, you'd just die.

An environment without S:CE would increase the number of combat decks
played. This would decrease the number of non-combat decks played, as
combat avoidance strategies that were previously viable would no
longer be reliable.

>As I said, the general level of combat could very well increase, but this
>envisioned environment of nothing but combat strikes me as unlikely as winning

Exactly. The person whose deck killed the best would win, because
nobody near him would have any minions left, whether they were combat
decks or not. OR, the person whose combat got the best draw; and
while that is a GOOD thing, to some degree, if it degenerates too far
it'll turn into a BAD thing.

> defense. If not, perhaps you've failed to consider deck design

Well that's the trick isn't it? We haven't begun to discuss the
problems when the Majesty deck is the prey, which requires a
different set of cards and different set of solutions than
when it is the predator. And since I can't make my deck
after I learn seating order, I have to balance my deck
against both of these situations, plus all the other decks
I'm liable to see in a variety of positions. My point is
that the S:CE and untap provides too many answers to
too many of those types of questions, and that's why
you see so many of them in so many decks (as was mentioned
recently in another thread). And that's why two of my
seven current decks pack them, and a third packs the
Form of Mist.

- Jason Bell

Messages.Author: Matt Latham
Messages.Body:
This is my final word on the subject.

I had a chance to play Jyhad for the first time in a long while yesterday.
We had quite an impressive turnout, so WW and VEKN must be doing something
right :)

I got to play with some Newsgroup notables like Wes, Noal, and Aaron, and
they and all the blokes that played were a great bunch, and I owe them
thanks for a wonderful day.

This all may have seemed like a Peter vs. Matt pissing match, but it
actually was a arguement over a difference in tournament philosophy. I have
fun in Jyhad by seeing the interesting deck builds people come up with, and
by socializing with these interesting deck builders I become a better, more
creative deck builder. So, to me, attending a tournament means I get to see
60 different decks, some I'll like and some I won't.

What I learned yesterday is that the fellas I was playing with could have
pulled out the most redundant or uncreative decks and I still would have
enjoyed myself immensely.

So, while I may not like clinging to certain deck types or over-reliance on
redundancy, I'll no longer socially revile those who choose to do so,
because they may not share my win condition.

While I may not have liked the tone of this discussion (I felt I was being
talked down to, and that's never fun) I learned a whole lot from it, so I
owe folks like Peter, Xian, Derek, and the rest a thank you.

Thank you.

Matt

Ah, I thought you meant "cookie cutter" as in "stamped out of a mold
in exactly the same way as every other cookie". Once you start from
the premise of "this will be a Shambling Hordes deck", you're probably
gonna play 10+ Hordes and a bunch of the same support cards as anyone
else who's designing a Shambling Hordes deck.

The problem with hating "cookie cutter" decks as you describe them,
as I wrote before, is that what seems like an obvious archetype to
one person may not be to another, and the obvious archetypes only
become more and more numerous over time. ie, four years ago, playing
Temptation of Greater Power/stealth-parity-shift was probably not at
all an "obvious archetype", but now it is. Likewise, six years ago,
Tzimisce intercept-combat didn't even exist; now it's an obvious
archetype.

> And no, tournaments werent always as you described. For years, Jyhad was such a pocket game that you were lucky
> to have 5 people within 50 miles of you who played. So tournaments at major cons were more for meeting and
> playing with new people rather than gotta win gotta win gotta win. Also, we didn't have archetypes per say (I
> remember the splash weenie voter and weenie presence made the first time they were played...) so creativity and
> unusuality were the name of the day.

I guess your experience has differed from mine on this. I've been
playing since late '94 or early '95, and every group I've ever played
in has taken the viewpoint that games define winning because it's what
makes them what they are, and that they should be played to try to win.
If you're just bouncing the volleyball back and forth over the net,
you're not playing the game, right?

The major-convention tournaments I've been to were the same way. Yeah,
it's always fun to meet and play with new people - games are about social
interaction, you bet - but they're about social interaction *within the
framework* of the game's victory conditions.

If I recall correctly, we all knew about Malk stealth-bleed and Ventrue
presence-vote and weenie vote push from just about day one. Not to
mention Nosferatu and Brujah potence rush combat, etc etc... there have
always been archetypes, and you can either play within them or try to
come up with things that people haven't seen before, but again, the
longer the game exists, the fewer things there are that people haven't
seen before. (Back in the day, it wasn't unusual to go to some other
town and play Brujah Immortal Grapple pot/cel rush and have your
opponents need to read Immortal Grapple several times before understanding
that they couldn't play Majesty. I think just about everyone knows what
IG does now...)

get an Express Exit.

logical... block the first bleed, they Majesty, untap, and call a vote

after a block.

A vote deck only has so many bleed modifiers in it.

Let's look closer at this. You've made your first rush on per above.
You've had a pretty decent card-flow, but that's OK. After you've
played Bums/TS/FoD/IG/Blur/Taste you're 16.7% of the way through your
deck. Now, if your deck is 20% IG (the standard amount, as far as i
can tell. Correct me if I'm wrong), you will normally *not* have a
second IG on hand at this point. If my vampire plays Skin of Steel
(even inferior could be enough in this case), it can play Majesty on
the second round of combat. This would leave me with an alive vamp
rather than a torporized one - quite important against the first rush.

This is of course just an example. As long as things run as one hopes
they would, then yes, you'll be able to cycle IG decently well.
However, as I'm sure anyone who has played a Pot Rush deck knows,
sometimes you're out of luck. Having to spend more IG than usual
increases the chance of not getting enough IG. It's not an incredibly
serious problem (the way running out of rush is), but if just a few
rushes fail, you may be in trouble.

The current discussion notwithstanding, there are also more types of
decks using IG than weenie potence rush. Nosferatu and Lasombra
toolboxes are just a two examples. They would have nowhere near the IG
density of potence weenie deck, and so their chance of replacing IG
would be correspondingly smaller

>Please show an example of S:CE getting stronger

You get a chance to play it second round if you didn't go to torpor on
the first round and the guy rushing you didn't have a second IG. For a
specific example: Ventrue with Skin of Steel + Majesty (more on that
below).

>Thank you for showing me how S:CE (Earth Meld) was weakened by the
>DotB errata. Now, thanks to the errata, S:CE can no longer inflict massive amounts
>of unpreventable damage. This is a good thing.

Yeah. You have to settle for a single point from Catatonic.

And I agree, S:CE+DotB (for offensive use) was weakened by the ruling.
S:CE as defence (against DotB) was strengthened by the same rule, as
you don't suffer the damage from DotB any more. I think the second
case was more common than the first, which resulted in a small overall
strengthening of S:CE.

>So what you are really saying is that Fortitude beats IG. I agree.
>You will still be pressed until you run out.

Before the ruling, this was totally true. Now, it's possible that the
rushing deck runs out of IG's before you run out of prevent.

>If it is pot cel IG you
>probably will run out of Fortitude before the round ends. If you are going to
>say that superior Skin of Steel prevents all strikes in a round, Then
>the cheapest Ventrue you are going to be playing with are Heather Florent or
>Nakova. Both of these are six caps. You should be getting rushed with
>two vampires for the price of one of these.

Possibly, but since I'm likely playing with the three 7-8 cap princes
anyway, at least *they*, (who are more important than the weenies) get
a better chance to survive. Always something.

>S:CE still gets mangled by IG. You haven't proved how it doesn't.

It does, yes. But not *quite* as badly as before.

>> Vampires with enough blood on them to stay out of torpor on the first
>> round also get a better chance of surviving the combat.
>
>If you can take 6 to 9 points of damage on round one, then you are
>able to survive at least your first IG Rush combat.

Pardon? The IG has a press on superior, and if you use Cel, you have
flashes. Unless I can press against, you just go to second round and
beat some more. This is where the ruling helped - unless you have a
second IG, I can now S:CE.

>> But yes, vampires that go to torpor on round one anyway are just as
>> f*cked.
>
>Are you agreeing or disagreeing with me here?

I'm agreeing in that vampires that don't survive round one anyway
don't get any bonus from the ruling on IG. Disagreeing on that would
be inane, as the change doesn't affect first round at all. However,
vampires that *can* survive round one (one way or the other) get a
chance of playing S:CE on round two, unless grappled again.

>> I never claimed S:CE received a *major* boost. But I think it's there,
>> and, especially for Ventrues packing a bit of fortitude, a noticable
>> one.
>
>Please demostrate how it is the S:CE that saves the Ventrue and not
>the fortiude.

It's the combination. Just fortitude doesn't cut it (you'll be pressed
until you run out). Just S:CE doesn't cut it (you'll be mangled on
round one). The two of them together can save you.

And a note for the record: I'm not claiming S:CE is unbeatable. Not at
all. A potence weenie deck will likely smear you all over the
countryside. But I can't for the life of me understand how anyone can
argue that it didn't get any advantage from the rulings (and I realize
you don't claim this - your argument that the improvements were
*negligible* is a far more interesting one. I personally think the
improvements were small but noticable, especially in some decks.)

Speaking as the guy who plays, pretty much, only Rush decks in competetion,
Derek is not off base here. If you are playing an IG Rush deck, the plan is to
kill your opponent on the first round, and most of the time (barring
Fortitude), it works. You need to go either heavy POT (Nosferatu) and stack up
TS, FoD, and US (7 points) for a killer first round strike, or POT/cel (Brujah)
with TS, US, Blur (8 points, assuming no CEL). Some would even advocate pot/CEL
and use TS, US, Blur for 7 points. Adjust according to taste and/or need. And
if all else fails, you have Disarm. If this doesn't kill them on round one, you
might have to press into a second round to finish them off--that is why you
play with 12 IG in your deck.

If you are playing a Rush deck that can't reliably torporize an opponent in one
round (again, barring Fortitude), then you aren't playing an effective Rush
deck. Sure, sometimes things don't go according to plan (you don't draw the
right cards, they have unforseen damage prevention) and you need to press. So
you play another IG. Generally, however, you only need one per combat, 'cause
your opponent is dead on the first round.

When the 7/7 errata fixed IG, yeah, I grumbled and complained for a few days,
but then I just tweaked my deck to take out the extra pressess and replace them
with more FoD. And added a few more IGs. And my deck works great. And 90% of
the time, I torporize an opponent on the first round.

Not really--when originally printed (in Jyhad), the duration of the "hand
strikes only" effect of an IG card was somewhat ambigious. At some point long
ago ('95?) it was ruled to last the entire combat. When it was reprinted in to
VTES, that concept carried across, and the VTES version (I'm not sure what the
Sabbat version says off hand) specifically says "entire combat". Somewhere
around the 7/7 errata (it may have been later on, however), it was ruled that

the fact that the "hand strikes only" aspect of IG only lasting for the current
round.

I guess at one point you could say that yes, IG had errata. At this point, it
does not, as the most recent printing of the card says what it does, and all
previous versions are to be read as the current printing.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

Jason wrote:
>>You seem to have conceded that effective, consistent,
and competitive S:CE defense consumes the entire
deck, or must ignore combat entirely. That concession,
if true (or even if it has ever met true), demonstrates
the point to my satisfaction.>>

Ok. Here is the deal with S:CE. Yes. It is a powerful effect that completely
dominates how combat works. I have said that before. I'll say that again. If,
from day one, had S:CE be designed differently (say as S:Round Ends instead),
combat would be *very* different than it is now. However, it wasn't. So we have
S:CE working the way it does and have to deal with it. Luckily, it isn't that
hard to deal with in a deck that needs to torporize.

What this means is that combat is VTES is, pretty much, an all or nothing
strategy--either you can stop S:CE and will torporize vampires left and right,
as that is what your deck is designed to to, or you can't stop S:CE, and
occasionally you'll torporize someone, but it doesn't really matter one way or
the other, as your deck isn't designed to torporize regularly.

If you are Rush deck, who ousts people by killing all of their vampires, and
defends itself by killing all of their vampires, and generally lives and dies
by its ability to torporize vampires, then S:CE isn't a problem--you have
designed your deck to get around it.

If you are not a Rush deck, then you have other ways of ousting your prey or
defending yourself such that an opponent playing S:CE isn't such a big deal. To
wit:

-A S+B deck: If your opponent blocks you and plays S:CE, you are happy, as you
aren't dead.

-A vote deck: If your opponent blocks you and plays S:CE, you are happy. And
then you play your own S:CE.

-Bloat deck: If your opponent blocks you and plays S:CE, you are happy, as you
aren't dead.

-An intercept deck: You generally work by stopping their actions, and that is
what you are trying to do. If they S:CE, you don't get hurt, and their action
is still stopped. Yeah, if they Majesty at superior, they can take another,
different action, which may or may not be significant. Usually it isn't. If you
are attempting to be an "Intercept/Burn" deck, you are destined for failure
anyways, as dedicated intercept (as a viable defense) requires, like, 33% deck
space for intercept, leaving not much space for combat. You could put in enough
to mess up folks who don't have S:CE in their hand when you get them (and you
get to see them play it before you play your strike) occasionally, but you are
never going to be able to reliably torporize with an intercept deck, S:CE or
no. Well, ok, as a caveat, a Gangrel intercept deck can torporize very
reliably, but they can do so with a bare minimum of cards and effort (8-10 Bone
Spur is all that a Gangrel intercept deck needs as killing power), and don't
have to play the necessary card until after they see if their opponent plays a
S:CE card.

-A Bruise/Bleed deck: Same problem as an intercept deck, in terms of being able
to torporize reliably, but you generally don't need to torporize so much
anyways. You bleed for 1, and if they don't block, you play a modifier. If they
do block, you are either stopped by S:CE or not, and it doesn't really matter
if they end up in torpor--you don't oust your prey by killing their vampires.
You oust them by bleeding them. You should have some IG or something in a B/B
deck, so you can kill folks occasionally, just to encourage them not to block
you, but in the long run, your combat is a secondary strategy to your
bleeding--it is there simply to encourage folks not to block.

>>You guys go ahead and believe that S:CE is balanced
because a completely dedicated deck can cope
with it, I'll be over here reading the other posts.>>

Yes, a completely dedicated deck can stop it quite nicely, such that if they
are played enough in a given environment, S:CE eventually disappears (as it is
useless). Decks that aren't completely dedicated to combat don't (or shouldn't)
care that their opponents play S:CE.

At this point in the evolution of this game, if one is designing a deck with
enough combat such that it is frustrating or debilitating when an opponent
plays S:CE and doesn't have a way to counter S:CE, one is making a grave
mistake in deck design.

Does S:CE completely dominate combat in VTES? Yes. Would the game be a very
different place if S:CE didn't exist? Yes. This being said, everyone knows
this, and can act accordingly. This means don't make a deck with 33% combat, no
way to stop S:CE, and then get upset when an opponent keeps playing Majesty.
Play decks that either can stop S:CE or don't care if its opponent plays S:CE.

(meaning I didn't dare intercept any action taken by a vampire with
Quietus, since we'd BOTH have died). I would have been DELIGHTED to
have more S:CE decks near me; I could've run them dry at no cost to
myself, torched their vamps, and run them over.

Before that, I played Brujah pitch. I sat next to S:CE several
different times, and each time I ran them out and began toasting their
vampires. (Two cross-table Dramatic Upheavals in the 1st and 3rd
round robbed me of my VPs, but that was my own fault for not including
some Delaying Tactics in the deck.)

Let's see. I've played Tzimisce intercept and made the finals,
erasing several S:CE decks along the way. I've played the Crypt
Machine, which totally ignores S:CE and CONSISTENTLY makes the finals
(in multiple peoples' hands). I've played an !Brujah vote/bruise
deck, which doesn't really care about S:CE either and has swept the
last 4 tables it's been played at. It has 18 combat cards and some
Templars for offense, but if you S:CE away from it, that's fine too.

In fact, for at least a year, maybe two, I can't remember playing a
deck in tournament, pickup, or otherwise and saying "damn! all that
S:CE is just screwing my deck!" Perhaps the way you build combat
decks is somewhat lacking? Perhaps you misunderstand the purpose of
combat? In any case, S:CE just doesn't impress me anymore. Too many
things beating up too many other things.

Actually, that's not true. I played a weenie THA rush deck that ran
flat into an S:CE wall once. But i'm under no delusions that such an
occurrence makes S:CE overpowered - just that my combat made no
allowance for S:CE other than "if I run into it, I lose".

-- Derek

Messages.Author: Ian Lee
Messages.Body:
>When the combat monkeys are telling you THEY
>don't think S:CE is overpowered... and they're the ones who get hurt
>worst by it...

This may be a different topic than what has been argued recently.

There is such a thing as light (offensive) combat. For instance, how can you
be toolboxy without some combat component?

If you focus your deck against S:CE, it better not be a problem. But, if you
don't, it is. One of the reasons I hope to see S:CE go away is that I think
I'd see a lot less IG as well.

I spent some time trying to run through what the metagame would be like without
S:CE based on the argument that combat would be king and certain combat clans
would rule.

I started with the idea that ANI/FOR/PRO would be the dominant strategy (not
just among combat but overall, since combat *had* to be the only viable way to
go). I looked at it against Assamite combat and (!)Brujah combat first. I
eventually concluded that the Assamites could still go, but they would have to
go to a close range, Disease/Thin Blood based strategy. Potence/Celerity just
couldn't get around Drawing Out the Beast, Scorpion Sting, Skin of Steel or
Flesh of Marble, aggropoke.

Next, I started looking at the possibilities not brought up a while back
matched up against the (!)Gangrel. Tzimisce can damage prevent with Horrid
Form and aggropoke. And, they have Blood of Acid, which neither Skin nor Flesh
will deal with. Lasombra will play more Entombments. !Malks more Comas. Etc.

So, either (!)Gangrel weren't going to dominate in combat or they were, but
others could still find ways to survive or hit back. Some of these options
didn't seem to take much in the way of card slots where the 4 card combo
obviously did.

The eventual conclusion I came to was that decks would not become entirely
combat oriented. The ubercombat deck still had to have just the right cards.
Fortitude and other damage prevention beat it. Enough other strategies went
even on it, while using far less cards. Obedience, Voice of Madness, Secure
Haven still dealt with rush. Lots of effects can deal with intercept. So,
getting into combat is not automatic. And, amusingly, Scorpion Sting becomes
key to stop S:Dodge, which is tons more interesting to me than a metagame of
"Grapple?".

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Ian wrote:
>>There is such a thing as light (offensive) combat. For instance, how can you
be toolboxy without some combat component?>>

You can be, and there are, but when playing such a deck, it isn't so tragic if
your opponent plays S:CE--you are playing a toolbox deck that does a little bit
of everything, so you aren't relying on torporizing your opposition. Sure, if
it comes up and you can pull it off, that is great, but if your opponent keeps
playing S:CE on you, and you have no counter, you can always fall back on the
other aspects of your deck. Yeah, it is a pain in the ass if you get blocked,
play Trap, Torn Signpost, Fists of Death, and try to hit them with a Burning
Wrath, just 'cause you had them all in your hand at one time, and they just
play Majesty, but unless your deck revolves around this strategy (killing
stuff), what does it matter? The point of a toolbox deck is that it is prepared
for everything. If your combat angle falls flat because you are facing a heavy
S:CE opponent, just give up the combat angle for the time being and move on.
Intercept their actions, bleed them, or whatever. Just say "Well, the combat
isn't going to work against this guy" and move on.

>>If you focus your deck against S:CE, it better not be a problem. But, if you
don't, it is.>>

But it isn't a problem, 'cause it doesn't matter if they S:CE. If you have a
smattering of combat in a toolbox deck, and you are faced with S:CE, just
ignore the combat. Use the combat cards in fights just to cycle them, and hope
that they don't have blasters, erm, Majesties. Don't worry about it. Unless
your deck *needs* to torporize someone on every action (in which case it should
be designed to counter S:CE), combat should be a sideline--sometimes it will
work, sometimes not, but if not, it shouldn't really matter.

Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija <pd...@aol.comANTISPAM> wrote in message
news:20010628213230...@ng-fq1.aol.com...

> Jason wrote:
> >>That's an awfully small corner to live in for the claim

> second round vs. IG). This is just bizarre that I'm

>

into
> making Rush decks viable and competetive than anyone on this newsgroup,
and can
> say with fair certainty that a Rush deck that cannot put 90% of the
vampires it
> attacks in to torpor on the first round of combat, it just isn't going to
work.

And doesn't that strike you as a design flaw? Only extremely focused
('degenerate', if you will) combat decks will work. Most other archetypes
can afford to fail more 10% and still work quite adequately. A S&B deck
might have nearly half of it's bleed actions deflected, and even more than
that intercepted, yet it can still manage to oust it's prey: one bleed is
sometimes enough, and it doesn't have to be the first one.

> Really. Yeah, sometimes you run into fortitude that can be a problem.
Sometimes
> you run into a lot of manuvers that can be a problem. Most of the time,
> however, you run into either S:CE or nothing (once the IG hits the table)
as
> combat defense.

And then the question is: what does it take to make such a deck? Due to
S:CE, the most reliable way to do it is IG. All other options (Hidden
Lurker, Fast Reaction, Psyche!, Telepathic Tracking, Guard Dogs, Thoughts
Betrayed... am I missing any?) have bigger costs (in blood, oportunity
and/or disciplines) and/or more limited effects (and maybe more importantly,
all cost more than Majesty). That coupled with the sheer brutality of pot
combat makes it by far the best option against S:CE.

So it is a very small corner indeed, because the best way to cope with
combat is S:CE (meaning: it eliminates 90% of possible combat decks - note
that I say 'possible', not 'viable', since many decks would be viable if it
were not for S:CE), and the best way to deal with S:CE is IG (meaning: IG
can deal with 90% of decks using S:CE, while other options are often less
efficient due to increased costs or moving parts).
How often do you see any of those other S:CE hoser cards played by combat
decks with acess to IG?

Compare that with other combat defenses:
- dodge can be countered by pressing, additional strikes, Scorpion Sting,
Skin Trap, Veil of Silence. Any combat deck can include at least some of
these, and they usually have a similar cost to the dodge itself. There's
little point in doing so though, since IG can do it also _and_ it can deal
with S:CE, while none of these do.
- damage prevention can be countered by pressing until they run out, steal
blood effects, unpreventable damage. Again, any combat deck can include some
of these, and it's costs are quite reasonable vs. the damage prevention
cards (Skin of Rock mirrors Undead Strength nicely).
- maneuvering to long can be dealt with by using long range strikes,
maneuvering back, or DotB. Again, no big deal.

If we didn't have IG, wouldn't S:CE become the only option for combat
defense?

This does look like the infamous X/anti-X situation that VtES should so
gracefully avoid.

<snip>

> How many cards are you talking? If it is close to the 10/10 split I
mentioned
> above, I assure you that yes, it can bollux a Rush deck, but it makes your
deck
> *much* less effective against non combat decks, and makes you a sub
optimal
> choice for a competetive field, unless you *know* that you are going to be
> playing against a large number of combat decks.

Not really. I once made a weenie Ventrue bleed deck (only weenie deck I ever
made, actually). It included lots of Majesty and Skin of Steel/Skin of Rock
as combat defense. I could cycle those cards on any 'normal' combat (anytime
it got blocked), though it didn't need to do so. Sure, it does not have a 0
cost to include that many of those cards in a deck, but they can be made
part of the deck's mechanics against other non-combat decks - for example,
if you intend to intercept your predator's actions, you'll probably enter
combat quite often enough to cycle those cards if needed be.

Of course, this is all academic, since we do have S:CE, and it is not going
away. :-/

Flux

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
On 29 Jun 2001 18:42:03 GMT, cur...@aol.com (Ian Lee) wrote:

>>When the combat monkeys are telling you THEY
>>don't think S:CE is overpowered... and they're the ones who get hurt
>>worst by it...
>
>This may be a different topic than what has been argued recently.

It's a different topic, but it's related in its own way.

>There is such a thing as light (offensive) combat. For instance, how can you
>be toolboxy without some combat component?

yes, but what purpose does that combat serve in your deck?

I think this is possibly another focus that people are missing. I
consider light combat to be a deterrent against heavy combat. Against
a heavy combat deck, if my deck is purely defensive, I'll run out and
die eventually, and the combat deck KNOWS that he can take a free run
at me whenever he has the Rush cards, or that he can bleed me for 1
repeatedly and I won't dare block. If I have some "surprise" combat
in the deck, even if it's something as simple as Lucky Blow, then my
actions are no longer predictable. Hasina Kesi, for example, can no
longer Rush me freely, as a Lucky Blow sends her to torpor. 2-blood
vamps can't afford to pay for a Blur. (countless other examples).

If my deck is all S:CE/dodge/prevent, I'm totally dependent on the
defensive combat working for me. Any deck that punches for more than
1 is a problem, and it's possible that even decks that punch for 1 are
a problem (if I'm using a lot of blood off my guys).

If someone is including light combat in their deck and expecting it to
consistently kill people whenever they whip it out... they're sadly
mistaken. Devoting only a small portion of your deck to anything puts
you more at the mercy of what's around you. For example, a vote deck
that includes just PAs and Praxis Seizures is totally at the mercy of
table votes and the Edge, but also doesn't have a whole lot of card
slots taken up. Adding Bewitching Orations increases your
effectiveness, but takes more slots. Adding Bribes, Voter Cap, etc...
still more slots.

Five .44s in your deck is a good token deterrent, but it isn't going
to beat combat defense, and it isn't going to save you from real
combat. It -does- make people think twice about entering combat with
you, which is really all you can ask out of 5 slots in your deck.

>If you focus your deck against S:CE, it better not be a problem. But, if you
>don't, it is. One of the reasons I hope to see S:CE go away is that I think
>I'd see a lot less IG as well.

(headshake) Potence needs to keep people from dodging just as much as
it needs to keep people from playing S:CE -- and it needs to keep
people from playing those dicky close-range strikes like Bonecraft,
Entombment, etc. The IG quota might go down from 12 to 8 in a deck,
but you'd still see plenty.

pot/CEL, on the other hand, doesn't care much about Dodges due to its
reliance on Blur, but can be somewhat more vulnerable to S:CE. (Idle
note: converting S:CE to "strike: round ends" would make pot/CEL
decks downright lethal, as all those Flashes and Psyches suddenly end
up serving a new purpose: to press.)

>Next, I started looking at the possibilities not brought up a while back
>matched up against the (!)Gangrel. Tzimisce can damage prevent with Horrid
>Form and aggropoke. And, they have Blood of Acid, which neither Skin nor Flesh
>will deal with. Lasombra will play more Entombments. !Malks more Comas. Etc.

!Malks won't be playing much Coma. I can find a number of better
things to do with 3 blood - notably, pull 2 of it off with a Blood
Doll and buy a .44.

And speaking of .44s, what about weaponry? With no S:CE, the
Assamites would possibly be almost untouchable. pack Disguised
Weapons and .44s, and a stack of Blurs. Season to taste with
Pursuit/Flash. Now you can outmaneuver everyone and shoot for lots,
and Dodge really doesn't do very well against superior CEL. If the
Gangrel play DotB, Disease at superior negates the Scorpion Sting
strike totally and you're fine. You still can't use the .44, but the
Blurs combined with the +1 strength from DotB will force them to have
(and use) superior Fortitude. Most likely result: a number of "drawn"
combats until someone doesn't get the Disease or DotB in hand.



Messages.Author: Johan Lundstrom
Messages.Body:
X_Ze...@email.msn.com (XZealot) wrote:

>Here is the problem with your arguement. You keep stating that S:CE
>got more powerful because you are packing Fortitude. Fortitude contains
>no S:CE.

Well, duh!

>It is mainly used for damage prevention. You cannot support
>your case that S:CE is more powerful if you use Fortitude. That is

I disagree. I'll re-iterate my point: Fortitude alone doesn't cut it.
The combat deck will press until you run out. And before the change in
IG, Fortitude + S:CE didn't cut it either, because IG lasted for the
whole combat. Now, however, the combat guy must play IG *every round*,
or you will S:CE. Thus, S:CE got *much* more useful, i.e. powerful, in
*combination* with Fortitude.

>That is like saying the Volkswagen Rabbit
>is the fastest car in the world if you strap it to the space shuttle. Do you
>follow what I am saying?

I see your point, but I don't agree.

It's like saying a bike works better when there's air in the tires.
You can use it with a flat on a tire, but when the road is bumby, it
won't be pleasant.

Bike=S:CE, tires=Fortitude, bumpy road=Pot Rush.

Responding, "oh, you're only talking tires here" doesn't cut it.

>You are right. Any deck that fails to do what it was designed to do,
>usually is in trouble.

Yup. And the ruling on IG made it more difficult for the deck to do
what was designed to do.

>> The current discussion notwithstanding, there are also more types of
>> decks using IG than weenie potence rush. Nosferatu and Lasombra
>> toolboxes are just a two examples. They would have nowhere near the IG
>> density of potence weenie deck, and so their chance of replacing IG
>> would be correspondingly smaller
>
>Also true, but not relavent to the arguement of how the ruling on IG
>made S:CE stronger.

What?! The fact that S:CE, after the change in IG, can help the deck
survive instead of going to torpor even when grappled on round 1, is
not *relevant*?! Then what is, pray tell?

>> You get a chance to play it second round if you didn't go to torpor on
>> the first round and the guy rushing you didn't have a second IG. For a
>> specific example: Ventrue with Skin of Steel + Majesty (more on that
>> below).
>
>Once again, Your fortitude arguement is moot. What you are really
>saying is not that S:CE got stronger but the Ventrue did. Please defend S:CE
>not the Ventrue (that's Rob Tresure's Job)

If a ruling makes card A very useful in combination with card B, while
neither A nor B is enough on their own, then saying "Oh, but that's
just B's doing", is no good.

A=S:CE, B=Fortitude.

And anyway, Fortitude *isn't* the only way to go to round 2 even after
being grappled on round 1. Everyone who has argued for Pot rush decks
puts the damage at 6-8 in the first round, and that's when the whole
combo is in place. I'm sure Anson on turn 1 will be a disgustingly
common sight from now on, and he can survive round 1. Since your
combat deck likely does *not* yet have a second IG, he can Majesty on
round 2, surviving the combat.

>I would contend that S:CE was weakened far more by the DotB errata
>than it was strengthen by either or both of the IG and Dotb errata.

I disgree, as the recepient of the DotB damage was likely as not also
a S:CE deck. And although DotB+S:CE was disgusting to be on the
receiving end of, it didn't make for a good deck. DotB existed in many
more decks than just DotB+S:CE.

>> >S:CE still gets mangled by IG. You haven't proved how it doesn't.
>>
>> It does, yes. But not *quite* as badly as before.
>
>Only if backed with Fortitude.

And whenever the damage is not enough to sink the vampire on turn 1.

>BTW, Do you see many disarms in your group?

Not that many. It's probably *the* most sought-after card in the game.
And I don't see huge amounts of them in most posted decks, either.

And anyway, as Peter Bakija said, sending the vampire into torpor with
blood on it isn't good enough. It will leave torpor and you have to
beat it down again.

>> Pardon? The IG has a press on superior, and if you use Cel, you have
>> flashes. Unless I can press against, you just go to second round and
>> beat some more. This is where the ruling helped - unless you have a
>> second IG, I can now S:CE.
>
>I don't disagree with you there. When did you discover this errata
>which has been in effect for at the very least a year or two?

When it first came on, obviously. But it's now that we're discussing
it.

And this is what I've been trying to say all along. S:CE got more
useful/more powerful when IG was errata'ed. It's not impossible to
beat in any way, but it became somewhat more difficult, particularly
with fortitude involved and when the vamp is big with lots of blood.

>IG was broken before. Now it has been fixed.

So you agree it was better before? What was it better against? Combat
Ends, for one thing. So now it's less good against S:CE than it was.
Therefore, S:CE became more powerful.

Do we even disagree here?

>Once again, this is a fortitude arguement not a S:CE arguement. The
>errata to IG was nessasary in the extreme.

See above.

>> >Please demostrate how it is the S:CE that saves the Ventrue and not
>> >the fortiude.
>>

Replacing IG with SS, nothing else changing, would be incredibly interesting to
me. Replacing IG with DOtB/SS/SoS/claws also sounds interesting. Combat is
currently largely dictated by the play of 1-2 cards. I want to see combat
where maneuvers and presses always matter, where each player is playing 3-4
important cards on a regular basis when a combat matters.

I think Peter says in one of these posts that the game is currently balanced.
I believe there are a number of balance issues, though the game as a whole is
pretty balanced. On an individual action level, I find combat, often, to be
the least interesting element of the game rather than the most interesting, as
it should be. Clans are not balanced against each other, disciplines are not
balanced against each other, discipline combinations are not balanced, but this
is getting off topic. Eliminating S:CE is no more likely to upset the balance
than introducing a new expansion. Players adjust, and they adjust to what
wins.

like TT and Perfect Clarity, but they're doing it slowly and it could
probably be done faster and more efficiently with a change to the base
rules, IMHO.

S:CE - Deflection.

acting minion could do against it until FN. That's why I once proposed a
card that would be played by the acting minion to burn the deflection, at
the cost of the action (I proposed that combat were started, because I was
afraid that S&B decks would abuse it otherwise). I was pretty happy when I
saw Contigency Planning in FN, it seems balanced just right (I don't play
bleed decks very often so I haven't tried it yet. Besides, right now
deflections aren't very popular around here anyway).

Flux

Hello!

I've just recently found this newsgroup, so please bear with me. I followed the thread above
trying to understand the heated discussion about S:CE (No matter whatever errata has
changed anything or not). Anyway, the discussion rang a bell about 'cards are broken so
you may only play with a limited amount of the' -complaints, so I tried to remember when
my playgroup had gotten mad about my opverpopulating my deck with S:CE, and realized
it never happened. My friends got thoroughly disgusted with my overuse of Auktarsis Persecution.

So, where does S:CE come in here?

One of my earliest deck-themes was weenie-hordes, packing the deck with Praxis Seizures,
Auktarsis, Archons, permament intercept, Flack Jackets and guns. Mastercards always around
20 with half of it Chimestry and one third Blood Dolls. Mass Reality, wake-cards and Progeny
filled the deck to the 90-limit.

I used to LOVE people stacking their decks with S:CE. They got weak on intercept and of course
kept my weenies alive during my build-up phase. However, I dreaded anything resembling manouver
and IG - for obvious reasons. After half the round I'd start jumping minions with my archons
equipped with +2 guns and bleed with the rest. At that time I seldom had less than 10 vamps out
and usually around fifteen. And yes, I spent a lot of time hunting and resquing from torpor, but
Auktarsis denies the other players from gaining VP:s and it's just so fun to get through two of
them
for fifteen pool each during one turn :)

Only after abandoning the deck-theme above did I see a valid reason for playing S:CE, but liking
weenies I still don't see S:CE as a problem. Ok, you stack up twenty of them I still empty your
hand of them each turn with one-bleeds with four or so vamps. If you don't block I just stay
untapped with the rest - I can live with only bleeding for 4 :) I still dread the rabid madman
coming after my small innocent weenies with a torn signpost hunting for a wrestling-match.

Sten During

You did need the Dog Pack to keep the second vampire from S:CE out of the
second combat. If you have a Dog Pack on Gitane, then there are only twoo
ways out of the second combat: you press to end the trap or you torpor Gitaine.
If you cannot do either of these, then you will eventually run out of
damage prevention and get sent to torpor.

It is a moot point now as the change to DotB makes this combo ineffective
and probably for a good reason.

Interesting thread, maybe should be retitled The Place of combat and
SCE in VTES. My views about all this have changed recently, for two
reasons:

[1] it has become much easier to make a viable combat deck from the
TACTICAL point of view. This has thrown the strategic inadequacy of
some new and not-so-new players into painfully-sharp relief. IMO
there's a danger that people just coming into the game will see
rush-combat as only a spoiling tactic because that's what it is when a
rush deck is played in a strategically-naive manner.

[2] i've actually played in an all-combat tourney in Southampton
[January this year IIRC]. i came second in the final [Malky OOT
rush/rotshreck], Barney won [big titled Gangrels] and Rob [Tzimisce
monsters] also got more VPs than me during the day. But you know what,
it was actually quite boring - one really missed the stealth/bleed and
vote decks, not to mention the funny off-the-wall stuff. Maybe the
moral is similar to something Tom kassel once wisely said, to the
effect that the last thing a rush-combat decks wants is a Fair Fight;
you want to BULLY people, was the gist of Tom's post, and in that
context SCE is the equivalent of running off to tell the teacher, so
an essential element of play balance as Peter and co are, i think
rightly, saying.
